lessons.title: Reusable subproblems and sufficient states
lessons.summary: Caching saves work only when the same subproblem is requested repeatedly.
lessons.body:
Dynamic programming (DP) is a way of solving a problem by breaking it into smaller subproblems, solving each subproblem **once**, storing the answer, and reusing it whenever the same subproblem comes up again.

That's it. The rest is learning to spot when it applies and how to describe each subproblem well.

The name is famously unhelpful. Richard Bellman developed the method in the 1950s, partly while working at RAND. "Programming" meant planning, as in a schedule or a table of decisions, not writing code. In his 1984 autobiography Bellman said he chose "dynamic" because it conveyed multistage, time-varying decisions and could not be used in a pejorative sense, which helped him shield mathematical research from a Secretary of Defense, Charles Wilson, who disliked the word "research". Treat that as a later recollection: Russell and Norvig point out that his first paper using the term (1952) appeared before Wilson took office (1953).

## The two ingredients

Before reaching for DP, look for two things: subproblems that come up repeatedly, and a valid rule for building an answer from the answers to smaller subproblems.

### Overlapping subproblems

A naive recursive solution solves the **same** subproblem many times. Caching helps only when a lookup can hit. If every subproblem were new (as in merge sort, where each half is different data), caching would buy nothing: that is plain divide and conquer.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a shared stock pot
> A restaurant has three soups on the menu, and all three start from the same chicken stock. A sensible kitchen makes the stock once in the morning and ladles it into each soup. A kitchen that made a fresh pot of stock for every bowl would do the same work again and again.
>
> **How it maps:** each soup is a larger problem, the stock is a subproblem that several of them need, and the pot of finished stock is the cache. Making it once and reusing it is exactly what DP does with a repeated subproblem.
>
> **Where it stops:** stock goes off and every bowl uses some of it up. A stored DP answer is just a value: it never changes and can be read any number of times. And reuse only works when the subproblem is *exactly* the same; a merge sort that sorts different slices is like a kitchen whose soups share no ingredient at all.

### Optimal substructure

An optimal solution to the whole problem can be **built from optimal solutions to subproblems**. In a graph with nonnegative edge weights, every segment of a shortest path is itself a shortest path between its endpoints. If it weren't, you could replace that segment with a shorter one and improve the whole route.

Whether this holds depends on what the **DP state** (the information that identifies one subproblem) records. The **longest simple path** between two nodes in a general graph does not have it if the state is just the two endpoints: the longest path from A to C via B need not contain the longest path from A to B, because that piece might use nodes the rest of the path needs. Recording the set of visited nodes as well restores a valid recurrence, but there are exponentially many such sets. Longest simple path is NP-hard in general, while shortest paths with nonnegative weights have fast polynomial-time algorithms.

So a good state is **sufficient**: it holds every fact the rest of the problem depends on, and nothing about how you got there matters beyond what it records.

> [!note] Counting problems too
> "Optimal substructure" is phrased in terms of optimisation, but DP also counts things ("how many ways...?") and decides things ("is it possible...?"). The general requirement is that the answer for a state can be **combined** from answers for smaller states.

## Key takeaways
- Caching saves work only when the same subproblem is requested repeatedly.
- A valid state must retain every fact needed to combine subanswers safely.

## Further reading
- [CMU notes quoting Bellman’s retrospective account](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/academic/class/15210-f14/www/lectures/dp.pdf)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [MIT algorithms course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/)

questions.prompt: Merge sort and memoised Fibonacci both split a problem into smaller pieces recursively. Why does caching results help Fibonacci enormously but do nothing for merge sort?

options.text: Merge sort lacks optimal substructure
options.explanation: Merge sort does build the whole answer from correctly sorted halves. What it lacks is repetition: the property in question is overlap, not substructure.

options.text: Fibonacci's subproblems overlap (the same `fib(k)` is needed many times), whereas merge sort's halves are disjoint pieces of data that are each sorted only once
options.explanation: Correct. A cache only pays off when a lookup can hit. Standard range-indexed merge sort visits each input interval once; memoisation by interval therefore does not reuse work. Equal-valued intervals could share results under a different, content-based cache, with its own key costs. Naive Fibonacci repeats the same numeric states.

options.text: Caching only works for problems on integers, not arrays
options.explanation: The type of the input is irrelevant. DP is routinely used on strings, arrays, trees and graphs; what matters is whether subproblems repeat.

options.text: Merge sort is already O(n log n) on n items, so it cannot be improved
options.explanation: Merge sort's speed is not the issue: even a slow algorithm would gain nothing from a cache that never hits. Comparison sorting does have a worst-case lower bound proportional to n log n comparisons for n items, but that is a separate fact. Standard merge sort has no repeated input-interval subproblems for a cache to reuse, so caching only adds overhead.

questions.workedExample:
1. For these examples, repeated states and a valid combination rule make memoisation useful.
2. Merge sort on `[5, 2, 8, 1]` splits into `[5, 2]` and `[8, 1]`, then into single elements. Each subarray is a different slice and is solved exactly once.
3. `fib(5)` calls `fib(4)` and `fib(3)`; `fib(4)` also calls `fib(3)`. The same subproblem appears in several branches.
4. A cache turns repeated work into lookups. With no repeats, it's pure overhead.
5. This distinguishes the standard recurrences in this example; it is not a universal disjoint-versus-overlapping classification.

questions.prompt: Which problem’s optimal substructure fails if a path state records **only its endpoints**, without the visited vertices?

options.text: Shortest path between two nodes in a graph with positive edge weights
options.explanation: Shortest paths do have optimal substructure: any sub-path of a shortest path is itself a shortest path, or you could shortcut it.

options.text: Minimum number of coins to make an amount
options.explanation: This has optimal substructure: remove one coin from an optimal solution for amount a, and what's left is optimal for the amount a minus that coin's value.

options.text: Longest simple path (no repeated vertices) between two nodes in a general graph
options.explanation: Correct. The longest simple path from A to C through B may not contain the longest simple path from A to B, because that longer piece could use vertices the B-to-C part needs. Endpoint-only subanswers do not safely combine; a state that includes the visited set can support DP.

options.text: Length of the longest common subsequence of two strings
options.explanation: LCS has optimal substructure: the answer for prefixes `(i, j)` (the first i characters of one string and the first j of the other) is built from the answers for `(i-1, j-1)`, `(i-1, j)` and `(i, j-1)`.

questions.workedExample:
1. Optimal substructure means: optimal whole = combination of optimal parts, with the parts independent of each other.
2. Shortest path: if the best A→C route via B had a non-shortest A→B piece, replace that piece with the shorter one and the whole gets shorter: contradiction.
3. Longest simple path: try the same argument. Replace the A→B piece with a longer one... but that piece might pass through a vertex the B→C piece also uses, making the result not simple. The parts interfere.
4. Recording the visited set restores a correct recurrence but yields exponentially many possible states. Longest simple path is NP-hard in general, so no polynomial-time algorithm is known for it.
5. On a DAG there are no cycles, so the interference vanishes, and longest path becomes an easy DP (the later unit “Evaluate path recurrences on a DAG”).

lessons.title: Why naive Fibonacci repeats work
lessons.summary: Base cases stop the recurrence at zero and one.
lessons.body:
## Fibonacci: the classic example

The Fibonacci numbers start 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...: each one after the first two is the sum of the two before it. Written as a **recurrence** (a rule that defines each value from earlier values of the same sequence):

```formula essential
F(0) = 0
F(1) = 1
F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2)   for n ≥ 2
where
F(n): the nth Fibonacci number, counting from F(0) = 0
n: the position in the sequence, a whole number 0, 1, 2, ...
F(n − 1), F(n − 2): the two Fibonacci numbers just before position n
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: the first two values are 0 and 1; every later value is the sum of the previous two.
```

The first two lines are the **base cases**: without them the rule would never stop asking for smaller values. The definition translates directly into code:

```python
def fib(n):
    # Reject values outside the recurrence.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    # The first two positions are base
    # cases.
    if n < 2:
        return n
    # Both smaller answers contribute.
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
```

For a nonnegative whole number n it is correct, but it becomes expensive as n grows. Look at the call tree for `fib(5)`:

```
              fib(5)
           /         \
       fib(4)        fib(3)
       /    \        /    \
   fib(3) fib(2)  fib(2) fib(1)
   /   \   / \     / \
 f(2) f(1) ...    ...
```

`fib(3)` is computed twice, `fib(2)` three times and `fib(1)` five times. These are the **overlapping subproblems**. Notice the pattern: the smaller the argument, the more branches lead to it, so the repeats pile up near the base cases.

## How fast the work grows

Each call counts itself plus every call its two children make. So the call count follows a Fibonacci-like rule of its own: `fib(5)` makes 15 calls, `fib(30)` makes 2,692,537 and `fib(40)` about 331 million.

```formula reference
calls(n) = 1 + calls(n − 1) + calls(n − 2)
calls(n) = 2F(n + 1) − 1
where
calls(n): the total number of calls made by the naive fib(n), including the first one; calls(0) = calls(1) = 1, and the first line applies from n = 2
n: the nonnegative Fibonacci position asked for
F(n + 1): the Fibonacci number at position n + 1
In words: one call for the current value plus every call made for the two smaller values, which works out to twice the next Fibonacci number, minus one.
```

Because Fibonacci numbers grow by a factor of about 1.618 (the golden ratio) at each step, so does the work: ten more positions multiply the number of calls by about 123. This is **exponential** growth, even though there are only n + 1 distinct subproblems (positions 0 to n). Almost all of the calls repeat an answer that has already been worked out somewhere else in the tree.

## Key takeaways
- Base cases stop the recurrence at zero and one.
- The naive call tree repeats states and grows exponentially.

## Further reading
- [Python caching](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

options.text: `fib(5)`, because it is the first and largest recursive call
options.explanation: `fib(5)` is requested exactly once, by `fib(6)` itself. Large arguments sit near the root of the call tree, where there are few branches.

options.text: Every argument from 0 to 6 is requested exactly once
options.explanation: That is what a memoised version does. Without a cache, the naive function recomputes the same argument in every branch that reaches it.

options.text: `fib(1)`, which is requested 8 times
options.explanation: Correct. Each argument is reached by every branch that passes through it, and the number of branches grows as the argument shrinks. `fib(1)` is the most repeated: 8 times, against 5 for `fib(0)`, 5 for `fib(2)` and 3 for `fib(3)`.

options.text: `fib(3)`, because it sits in the middle of the tree
options.explanation: `fib(3)` is repeated (3 times), but smaller arguments are reached by even more branches. Repeats grow towards the base cases, not the middle.

questions.workedExample:
1. `fib(6)` asks for `fib(5)` and `fib(4)`. `fib(5)` asks for `fib(4)` again, so `fib(4)` is already requested twice.
2. Every request for `fib(k)` produces one request for `fib(k − 1)` and one for `fib(k − 2)`. So the number of requests for an argument is the sum of the requests for the two arguments just above it: the counts follow a Fibonacci pattern of their own.
3. Counting down from the top: `fib(6)` 1, `fib(5)` 1, `fib(4)` 2, `fib(3)` 3, `fib(2)` 5, `fib(1)` 8. (`fib(0)` is only reached from `fib(2)`, so it is requested 5 times.)
4. The smallest non-trivial argument is the most repeated. Altogether there are 25 calls for only 7 distinct arguments, which is the waste memoisation removes.

lessons.title: Cache Fibonacci answers
lessons.summary: Memoisation computes a state on demand, then reuses its answer.
lessons.body:
The previous unit showed that the naive Fibonacci recursion requests the same positions repeatedly. Keep the same recurrence and add a cache rather than changing the mathematical answer.

### Fix 1: memoisation (top-down)

Here n is the nonnegative Fibonacci position. Keep the recursion, but remember every answer. Before computing `fib(k)`, check the cache.

```python
def fib(n, memo=None):
    # Reject values outside the recurrence.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    # One fresh cache per top-level request.
    if memo is None:
        memo = {}
    # The first two positions are base
    # cases.
    if n < 2:
        return n
    # Compute a state only on a cache miss.
    if n not in memo:
        # Store the result for later
        # callers.
        memo[n] = fib(n - 1, memo) + \
                  fib(n - 2, memo)
    return memo[n]
```

Python has this built in:

```python
from functools import cache

# Repeated arguments reuse stored answers.
@cache
def fib(n):
    # Reject values outside the recurrence.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    # The first two positions are base
    # cases.
    if n < 2:
        return n
    # Both smaller answers contribute.
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
```

`functools.cache` is an unbounded cache, the same as `lru_cache(maxsize=None)`: it keeps every answer for the life of the function, keyed by the arguments.

In a cold-cache (initially empty), single-threaded `@cache` call with n of 2 or more, the body runs once for each value from 0 up to n; later requests hit the cache. The manual version does not cache its constant-time base cases. Counting integer additions and dictionary operations as unit cost gives **O(n) work and O(n) stored numbers**, plus recursive stack space.

The call tree collapses into a chain:

```
fib(5) -> fib(4) -> fib(3) -> fib(2) -> ...
   \         \         \
  fib(3)    fib(2)    fib(1)
  (hit)     (hit)     (hit)
```

## Key takeaways
- Memoisation computes a state on demand, then reuses its answer.
- A cold, single-threaded cache executes the Fibonacci body once per reachable argument.

## Further reading
- [Python caching](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

    # increments.

    # cases.

fib(10)

options.explanation: Correct. The body runs once per distinct argument: `0..10` is 11 values. The cache persists, so `fib(12)` only computes the two new values, 11 and 12.
Off by one: `fib(0)` is also a distinct state. `fib(n)` has n + 1 states (0 to n), so `fib(10)` has 11, not 10.
This assumes the cache resets between top-level calls. `@cache` lives on the function object, so `fib(12)` reuses all of `fib(0..10)`.

Those are the naive call counts for `fib(10)` and `fib(12)` taken separately (twice the next Fibonacci number, minus one: 2 × 89 − 1 = 177 and 2 × 233 − 1 = 465). A cumulative counter without caching would print 177 then 642, since the second call adds 465. With `@cache`, repeated calls return the stored value without running the body, so `calls` isn't incremented.

questions.workedExample:
1. `@cache` wraps `fib`: on a call it checks a dictionary keyed by `n`. On a hit it returns immediately, without running the body.
2. `fib(10)` recurses down to `fib(1)` and `fib(0)`; each of `0, 1, ..., 10` is computed exactly once. That's 11 body executions.
3. Every other call (for example the second request for `fib(8)`) is a hit and doesn't touch `calls`.
4. `fib(12)` calls `fib(11)` (new: +1), which calls `fib(10)` (hit) and `fib(9)` (hit). Then `fib(10)` (hit).
5. `fib(12)` itself is new: +1.
6. Total: 11 + 2 = 13.

lessons.title: Tables, rolling values and DP cost
lessons.summary: Bottom-up evaluation fills dependencies before reading them.
lessons.body:
Here n is the nonnegative requested Fibonacci position. Fibonacci at a position uses only the two preceding values. This unit changes how those values are evaluated and stored, while preserving the same answer.

### Fix 2: tabulation (bottom-up)

Turn the recursion inside out. Fill a table from the smallest subproblem upwards, so that every value you need has already been computed.

```python
def fib(n):
    # Reject values outside the recurrence.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    # The first two positions are base
    # cases.
    if n < 2:
        return n
    table = [0] * (n + 1)
    table[1] = 1
    # Both dependencies are already filled.
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        table[i] = table[i-1] + table[i-2]
    return table[n]
```

Same O(n) time, same O(n) space, but no recursion.

### Fix 3: keep only what you need

`table[i]` only looks back two entries, so the rest of the table is dead weight. Keep two variables:

```python
def fib(n):
    # Reject values outside the recurrence.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    a, b = 0, 1  # F(0), F(1)
    for _ in range(n):
        # Advance the two retained values
        # together.
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a
```

**O(n) additions, O(1) integer slots.** With Python’s exact integers, F(n) has Θ(n) bits: this loop uses O(n) bits and O(n²) bit work, while retaining the whole Fibonacci table uses Θ(n²) bits. This "keep only the last few rows" trick is a standard DP space optimisation you'll see again for grids and knapsack.

The table counts unit-cost arithmetic and integer slots rather than bits. In its naive-recursion row, φ is the golden ratio, about 1.618.

| Version | Unit-cost work | Extra slots |
|---|---|---|
| Naive recursion | O(φⁿ) | O(n) stack |
| Memoised | O(n) | O(n) |
| Tabulated | O(n) | O(n) |
| Two variables | O(n) | O(1) |

This gives the rule of thumb for the cost of any DP. The exact cost is the work summed over every DP state you evaluate; multiplying the number of states by the most work any one state needs gives a quick upper bound:

```formula reference
T ≤ S w_max
where
T: the total running time of the DP, in basic steps
S: the number of distinct states (subproblems) evaluated
w_max: the most work any single state does, not counting the states it looks up
≤: less than or equal to
In words: count the subproblems, multiply by the most work any one of them does on its own (not counting the lookups of other subproblems), and you have an upper bound on the running time.
```

For Fibonacci there are n + 1 states, each doing one addition, so the work is O(n). A DP with only n states can still be slow if each state scans many earlier states: that per-state work is the other half of the bound.

> [!tip] What the formula leaves out
> Add any preprocessing, the work to reconstruct the chosen solution, and the cost of arithmetic on very large numbers (operand bits) when they matter.

## Key takeaways
- Bottom-up evaluation fills dependencies before reading them.
- Two integer slots suffice for Fibonacci, but their bit sizes grow.
- Count states and transition work, including preprocessing and reconstruction.

## Further reading
- [Python caching](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

What are the time and extra space of this version?

1. Count the loop: `range(n)` gives n iterations.
2. Each iteration does one addition and a tuple assignment: constant work. So n iterations take time proportional to n: O(n).
3. Space: only `a` and `b` are kept. Each Fibonacci number needs just the two before it, so everything older can be thrown away: O(1) extra slots.

questions.prompt: A DP has states `best[i]` for `i` in `0..n`, and each state is computed as `min(best[j] + cost(j, i) for j in range(i))`, where `cost` is O(1). It runs instantly with n = 1,000 but takes far too long with n = 100,000. What is the best diagnosis?

options.text: It needs a cache: without memoisation it recomputes `best[j]` exponentially often
options.explanation: The table already stores every `best[j]`, so nothing is recomputed. Exponential blow-up is the naive-recursion problem, not this one.

options.text: The recursion is too deep for Python's call stack
options.explanation: This is a table filled by a loop, so there is no recursion to overflow. The slowdown is in the amount of work, not the stack.

options.text: 100,000 states is simply too many for any DP
options.explanation: 100,000 states with constant work each would take a fraction of a second. The number of states is not the problem; the work per state is.

options.text: Each state scans every earlier state, so the total work is quadratic: about five billion candidate transitions
options.explanation: Correct. State i tries i earlier values, so the total is 1 + 2 + … + n, about n² / 2. Going from 1,000 to 100,000 states multiplies the work by about 10,000, not 100.

questions.workedExample:
1. Count states: about 100,000 table entries, each stored once. Storage is not the issue.
2. Count the work per state: the generator tries every earlier index, so state i does i candidate transitions.
3. Add them up: 1 + 2 + … + n is about half of n squared. For n = 100,000 that is about five billion candidates; for n = 1,000 it is only about half a million.
4. A hundred times more states therefore means about ten thousand times more work. That is the signature of quadratic total work, even though each state is computed only once.
5. The fix is a better recurrence or a proved optimisation that avoids scanning every earlier state (for example a monotone queue, the convex hull trick or divide-and-conquer DP), not more caching.

Takeaway: always multiply the number of states by the work each state does.

lessons.title: Choose top-down or bottom-up
lessons.summary: Memoisation can skip unreachable states; dense tabulation may fill them.
lessons.body:
You have now seen the same Fibonacci recurrence evaluated recursively and iteratively. Choose the evaluation strategy by the reachable states, dependency order and storage requirements.

## Memoisation vs tabulation

Both can evaluate the same recurrence. They may visit different sets of states; they differ in **who decides the order**.

- **Memoisation** lets the recursion discover which subproblems are needed, on demand.
- **Tabulation** has you choose an order up front so that dependencies are always ready.

| | Memoisation | Tabulation |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | Top-down | Bottom-up |
| Order | Automatic | You choose it |
| Unneeded states | Skipped | Usually computed |
| Recursion limit | A risk | No issue |
| Space tricks | Hard | Easy |

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: two ways to cook a dinner
> One cook starts from the main recipe. Whenever a step says "add the sauce", they pause, make the sauce, label the jar and carry on; if the sauce is needed again, they use the jar. Another cook first works through a prep list in a planned order, so every sauce and stock is ready before the main recipe starts.
>
> **How it maps:** the first cook is memoisation: sub-recipes are made on demand and the labelled jars are the cache. The pile of half-finished recipes they must come back to is the recursion stack. The second cook is tabulation: the prep list is the evaluation order, and it must put every ingredient before the dishes that use it.
>
> **Where it stops:** a kitchen can often reorder prep steps freely, but a DP table order must respect every dependency exactly. And a prep list may make a garnish that nobody ends up using, which is the tabulation cost of filling unreachable states. Both cooks produce the same dinner: the evaluation strategy changes the order and the overheads, never the answer.

### When memoisation wins

- It's **easier to write**: take the recursive definition and add a cache.
- It computes **only reachable states**. If most of a huge state space is never visited, top-down can be far faster.
- The evaluation order can be awkward to work out by hand (trees, DAGs, odd dependency shapes). Recursion handles it for you.

### When tabulation wins

- **No recursive call-depth limit.** CPython usually starts with a recursion limit of 1,000 (`sys.getrecursionlimit()`), but configuration, existing call depth and previously cached answers affect when an error occurs. A cold deep recursive Fibonacci call can fail; the loop avoids that limit, though large exact answers still cost arithmetic time and memory.
- **Potentially lower overhead**: a dense array implementation can avoid recursive calls and dictionary lookups. Actual performance depends on representation and reachable states.
- It enables the **rolling-array** space optimisations, because you control exactly when old rows can be thrown away.

> [!warning] Mutable default arguments
> Writing `def fib(n, memo={})` "works" because Python evaluates the default once and shares it across calls. That is a well-known trap: the cache silently leaks between unrelated calls, which bites you as soon as the inputs change (for example, a memo keyed only on `i` for a function that also depends on a list argument). Use `None` as the default, or `@cache` on an inner function.

## Key takeaways
- Memoisation can skip unreachable states; dense tabulation may fill them.
- Iterative evaluation avoids recursive call-depth limits.
- A cache must have the right key and the right lifetime.

## Further reading
- [Python caching](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

questions.prompt: Your memoised recursive solution passes every test with input indices no larger than 500, but in production it crashes with `RecursionError` at index 5,000. The recurrence for input n only depends on smaller inputs. What is the most robust fix?

options.text: Switch from `@cache` to `@lru_cache(maxsize=128)`
options.explanation: A bounded cache evicts entries and can make the function slower or exponential again; it does nothing to reduce recursion depth.

options.text: Rewrite it bottom-up: loop `i` from the base cases up to n, filling a table in dependency order
options.explanation: Correct. Tabulation can evaluate the same recurrence but uses a loop, so there's no call stack to overflow. It can also avoid recursive calls and dictionary lookups; actual speed depends on the implementation and states visited.

options.text: Wrap the call in `try/except RecursionError` and retry
options.explanation: Retrying hits the same depth and fails again. Swallowing the exception doesn't produce an answer.

options.text: Memoisation can't handle n this large; the problem needs a different algorithm
options.explanation: The observed error concerns recursive evaluation depth. Iterative evaluation removes that limit; feasibility still depends on total states, transitions and value sizes.

questions.workedExample:
1. CPython normally starts with a recursion limit of 1,000; inspect the actual setting with `sys.getrecursionlimit()`. Existing depth and wrappers affect the observed threshold.
2. A top-down `f(n)` that calls `f(n-1)` is about n frames deep on the first call, so an initial index of 5,000 exceeds the usual configured limit.
3. Options:
   - `sys.setrecursionlimit(10_000)`: may help but is platform- and call-path-dependent; it does not reduce memory or work. Since CPython 3.11 most Python-to-Python calls avoid an additional C call, but native recursion can still matter.
   - Bottom-up: `for i in range(2, n + 1): t[i] = ...`. Constant recursive depth; the same recurrence’s transition work must still be counted.
4. Because the recurrence only depends on smaller indices, increasing i is a valid evaluation order, so tabulation is a mechanical rewrite.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
def ways(n, steps, memo={}):
    # A jump past the start cannot be a
    # route.
    if n < 0:
        return 0
    # The empty continuation is one
    # route.
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    # Compute a state only on a cache
    # miss.
    if n not in memo:
        # WARNING: steps is missing from
        # the key.
        memo[n] = sum(
            ways(n - s, steps)
            for s in steps)
    return memo[n]

print(ways(4, [1, 2]))
print(ways(4, [1, 2, 3]))
```

options.text: `5` then `7`
options.explanation: These are the correct answers to the two questions, but not what this code prints. The memo is shared between the calls and isn't keyed on `steps`.

options.text: `5` then `5`
options.explanation: Correct. The default `memo={}` is created once and shared by every call. The second call finds `memo[4] = 5` from the first call and returns it, ignoring the new `steps`.

options.text: `4` then `7`
options.explanation: With steps {1, 2} there are 5 ways to climb 4 (1111, 112, 121, 211, 22), not 4. And the second call can't compute fresh values because of the shared cache.

options.text: It raises `TypeError` because a dict can't be a default argument
options.explanation: Any object can be a default argument. The problem is subtler: mutable defaults are evaluated once at definition time and shared.

questions.workedExample:
1. Python evaluates `memo={}` once, when `def` runs. Every call that doesn't pass `memo` uses that same dict (and the inner calls don't pass it).
2. First call, steps {1, 2}: each count is the sum of the two below it, so the cache fills with 1, 2, 3 and 5 for 1 to 4 stairs. `ways(4, [1, 2])` prints 5, which is correct.
3. Second call, steps {1, 2, 3}: `4 in memo` is already true, so it returns the stored 5 without looking at the new `steps`.
4. The correct answer is 7 (1111, 112, 121, 211, 22, 13, 31), because a 3-step adds new routes.
5. The deeper lesson: the cache key must include **everything** the answer depends on, and the cache must live only as long as those inputs stay the same. Here `steps` changes the answer but isn't in the key. Fix: `memo=None` plus a fresh dict per top-level call passed explicitly to every recursive call, or `@cache` on an inner function that closes over `steps`.

questions.prompt:
You need `f(10**12)` for this function:

```python
def f(n):
    # Zero is the base case.
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    # Recurse on the rounded-down half
    # and third.
    return 1 + f(n // 2) + f(n // 3)
```

Which approach is practical?

options.text: Tabulate an array `t[0..n]` from 0 upwards
options.explanation: That needs 10¹² entries (terabytes of memory) and 10¹² iterations, even though almost none of those values are ever needed.

options.text: Plain recursion without a cache
options.explanation: The two branches overlap heavily (for example n // 6 is reached both by halving then thirding and by thirding then halving), so without a cache the work grows polynomially in n, far too much at 10¹².

options.text: Top-down memoisation with a dictionary
options.explanation: Correct. Only the values you get by repeatedly halving and thirding n (rounding down) are ever reached: a few hundred distinct states for an initial input of one trillion. Memoisation computes only reachable states, and the recursion is only about 40 calls deep, because 10¹² can be halved only about 40 times before reaching 0.

options.text: It can't be done; the state space is 10¹²
options.explanation: The nominal state space is 10¹², but the reachable state space is tiny. Confusing the two is exactly why top-down sometimes beats bottom-up.

questions.workedExample:
1. Which arguments are reachable? Start at n and repeatedly apply `// 2` or `// 3`. Rounding down twice in a row gives the same result as dividing once by the product and rounding down, so every reachable argument is n divided by some power of 2 times some power of 3 (rounded down), or zero.
2. n = 10¹² can be halved about 40 times and divided by 3 about 25 times before reaching zero, so there are at most about 40 × 26 such combinations: around a thousand candidate states. Many combinations give the same quotient; in practice there are 438 distinct values.
3. Memoisation computes each of those once: a few hundred additions, with recursion only about 40 calls deep.
4. Without a cache, the same quotient is reached along many different halve/third orders, so the call count explodes. A dense table would allocate 10¹² + 1 entries, almost none of them needed. (A carefully built sparse bottom-up order could also restrict itself to the reachable states.)
5. Rule of thumb: when the reachable states are a sparse subset of a huge range, prefer top-down.

questions.prompt: Which statements about memoisation (top-down) versus tabulation (bottom-up) are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: With the same per-state cost model and no eviction, both have the same asymptotic work when every state is reachable
options.explanation: Correct. Both evaluate each state once with the same work per state, so both are states × work. The differences are in constants, memory and ordering.

options.text: Tabulation makes rolling-array space optimisations easy because you control exactly when each row stops being needed
options.explanation: Correct. With an explicit loop order you know that row i only needs row i − 1, so you can discard the rest. Memoised implementations can also release values with dependency tracking, but plain unbounded caching does not do so automatically.

options.text: Memoisation is always faster because it skips unneeded states
options.explanation: Skipping unreachable states can save work, but actual speed also depends on recursion, hashing, representation and implementation. The same state set alone does not establish a universal speed ordering.

options.text: Tabulation requires you to choose an evaluation order in which every dependency is computed before it is used
options.explanation: Correct. This is the main extra design step bottom-up demands. Get it wrong and you read uninitialised cells.

options.text: Memoisation computes subproblems in a different order, so it can give a different answer
options.explanation: The recurrence defines the value of each state uniquely; order affects only when it's computed. A correct memoised and a correct tabulated solution always agree.

questions.workedExample:
1. Both strategies evaluate the same function on the same states. A state's value depends only on the recurrence, so the answers are identical.
2. Cost is states × work per state in both cases.
3. Differences:
   - Top-down: automatic order, skips unreachable states, but has call overhead and recursion depth limits.
   - Bottom-up: you pick the order, no recursion, arrays not hashes, and you can keep only the last row or two.
4. So "always faster" is false (it depends on reachability) and "different answer" is false (only the order differs).

lessons.title: Spot repeated states in real problems
lessons.summary: DP also solves counting and decision problems.
lessons.body:
## DP vs its neighbours

| Technique | Subproblems | Choice |
|---|---|---|
| Typical divide and conquer | Separate smaller inputs | Combine recursive results |
| Greedy | One per step | Commit locally |
| Typical DP | Reusable states | Combine feasible alternatives |

**Greedy** makes one locally best choice and never revisits it. It can avoid examining alternatives, but needs a proof that the local choice is safe. DP tries every option for each decision and keeps the best, which is why it handles problems where greedy fails (you'll see coin change with coins `{1, 3, 4}` in “Minimise the coins for an amount”).

## Where DP shows up in the real world

DP is not just an interview topic. A few systems that are DP at their core:

- **`diff` and `git diff`** are built on longest common subsequence and related edit-script algorithms.
- **Spell checkers and fuzzy search** use edit (Levenshtein) distance.
- **Bioinformatics** aligns DNA and protein sequences with Needleman–Wunsch and Smith–Waterman, both grid DPs.
- **Hidden Markov models** use Viterbi decoding to find the most likely hidden-state sequence; speech recognition is a classical application.
- **Network routing**: Bellman–Ford, used in distance-vector protocols like RIP, is DP over path lengths.
- **Query optimisers** in databases have long used DP to choose join orders (the System R approach).

## Why those recurrences can repeat work

For a right/down grid, going right then down reaches the same cell as going down then right. A naive recursion from either route therefore asks for the same remaining grid paths. Stair counts with one-step and two-step choices repeat in the same way as Fibonacci. In longest common subsequence, mismatching characters permit skipping from either string; different skip histories can reach the same pair of remaining prefixes. A cache identifies that repeated pair rather than remembering the whole skip history. Binary search follows only one smaller range, while ordinary merge sort visits distinct input intervals.

## Common pitfalls

1. **Caching without overlap.** Memoising standard merge sort by input interval adds overhead and does not reuse an interval; a content-based cache has different key costs and may reuse equal-valued segments. Check that subproblems actually repeat.
2. **A state that's missing information.** If the answer depends on something you didn't put in the cache key, the cache returns wrong answers. More in the next lesson.
3. **Forgetting base cases**, which leads to infinite recursion or off-by-one tables.
4. **Exponential numbers.** `F(1000)` has 209 digits. Python integers grow as needed. Fixed-width Java integer arithmetic wraps; signed integer overflow in C++ is undefined behavior, while arbitrary-precision libraries are available. Reduce modulo a value only when that is the requested output.

## Key takeaways
- DP also solves counting and decision problems.
- Greedy needs a proof that each committed choice is safe.
- Check overlap, sufficient state, base cases and numeric limits.

## Further reading
- [Selinger and colleagues: System R access-path selection](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs346/2014/selinger.pdf)
- [RIP distance-vector foundations](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2453)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [MIT algorithms course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/)

questions.prompt: In which of these would a naive recursive solution solve the **same subproblem repeatedly**, so that memoisation helps? Select all that apply.

options.text: Counting the monotone paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid, moving only right or down
options.explanation: Correct. Every path from a cell starts by going down or right, so the count for a cell is the count from the cell below plus the count from the cell to its right. Right-then-down and down-then-right both reach the same diagonal cell, so a naive recursion recomputes the same cells exponentially often.

options.text: Binary search for a value in a sorted array
options.explanation: Binary search follows a single path, discarding half the array each time. No subproblem is ever visited twice.

options.text: Finding the length of the longest common subsequence of two strings
options.explanation: Correct. `lcs(i, j)` branches to `lcs(i+1, j)` and `lcs(i, j+1)`, and both reach `lcs(i+1, j+1)`. There are only about m·n distinct states (m and n being the two strings’ lengths) but exponentially many recursive paths to them.

options.text: Merge sort
options.explanation: Each recursive call sorts a different, disjoint slice of the array. Nothing repeats.

options.text: The number of ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time
options.explanation: Correct. The last move is either a 1-step or a 2-step, so the number of ways for n stairs is the number for n − 1 plus the number for n − 2. That is the same shape as Fibonacci, with the same exponential overlap.

questions.workedExample:
Test each one by asking: "can two different branches of the recursion arrive at the same arguments?"

1. Grid paths: right-then-down and down-then-right both reach `(r+1, c+1)`. Yes.
2. Binary search: one branch per step, so no. A single path of O(log n) calls, where n is the array length.
3. LCS: skipping a char of A then B, or B then A, both reach `(i+1, j+1)`. Yes.
4. Merge sort: the left and right halves are different slices. No.
5. Stairs: `ways(n-1)` itself calls `ways(n-2)`, which `ways(n)` also calls directly. Yes.

The repeated ones are DP problems; the others are divide and conquer (or decrease and conquer).

lessons.title: Define states, transitions and base cases
lessons.summary: State definitions explain exactly which subproblem a table cell represents.
lessons.body:
The goal is to describe subproblems precisely enough that cached answers remain valid. A state is a contract: equal states must require equal answers.

Defining the state and recurrence is often the hardest part of a DP problem. A systematic method helps make those decisions explicit.

Here are five questions to answer, in order. Write the answers down in plain English before you write any code.

1. **State**: what does `dp[...]` mean, exactly?
2. **Recurrence**: how is one state computed from smaller ones?
3. **Base cases**: which states can be answered directly?
4. **Order**: in what order must states be evaluated?
5. **Answer and reconstruction**: which state holds the answer, and how do you recover the actual choices, not just the number?

Then add a sixth, quick step: **complexity**: count the states and the work per state.

## Step 1: define the state

The **DP state** is the set of parameters that describes a subproblem. It must capture **everything the future depends on**. Extra information can increase cost even when the state remains correct.

A good test: "If I know only these values, can I solve the rest of the problem optimally without knowing how I got here?" If yes, you have a valid state. If the answer also depends on something else (a previous choice, a remaining budget), that something must join the state.

Common state shapes:

| Input | Typical state |
|---|---|
| One sequence | prefix `i` or suffix `i` |
| Two sequences | pair `(i, j)` |
| Sequence, ranges | interval `(i, j)` |
| Items + budget | `(i, capacity)` |
| Tree | node `v` (+ flag) |
| Small set | bitmask |

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: saving a chess game
> To pause a chess game and resume it later, you don't need the list of every move played. You need the board, whose turn it is, and a few facts the board can't show, such as whether each side may still castle (a special king-and-rook move whose right is lost for good once that king, or the rook involved, has moved). The standard one-line notation for recording a chess position stores exactly that kind of information, not the move list.
>
> **How it maps:** the saved position is the DP state. The test "can I play on correctly from here without knowing how we got here?" is the sufficiency test. Leaving out castling rights is an under-specified state: two games with the same board but different rights would wrongly share one answer. Storing the full move list is over-specified: correct, but it makes almost every position look different, so nothing is reused.
>
> **Where it stops:** chess also has a draw rule, threefold repetition: a player may claim a draw when the same position occurs for the third time. That depends on earlier positions, which the saved position does not record, so a chess position is not a perfectly sufficient state. A DP state must be fully sufficient for its recurrence, and the same state is deliberately shared by many different routes that reach it.

Write the definition as a full sentence: "`ok[i]` is True if the suffix `s[i:]` can be split into dictionary words." Vague definitions ("`dp[i]` is the answer at i") are the root of most wrong recurrences.

## Step 2: the recurrence

Ask: **what is the first (or last) decision**, and what are the options? Each option is a **DP transition**: it leads from the current state to a smaller subproblem. Combine the results with whatever the question asks for:

- "minimum/maximum" → `min` / `max` over options
- "how many ways" → **sum** over options (they must be disjoint, or you'll double-count)
- "is it possible" → **or** over options

## Step 3: base cases

The smallest states, where no decision is left: an empty string, a zero weight limit, a single element. Also decide what an **impossible** state returns: `0` for counting, `False` for feasibility, `+∞` (positive infinity, a value worse than any real cost) for minimisation, and `−∞` (negative infinity, worse than any real profit) for maximisation. In Python these are `float('inf')` and `-float('inf')`. A `min` never picks `+∞` when a real option exists, and a `max` never picks `−∞`, so impossible options drop out automatically. Using 0 for an impossible minimisation state is a classic bug: 0 beats every real cost, so the impossible option wins.

For counting, the empty remainder counts as **one** way: "do nothing more". Every count is ultimately a sum of those ones, so setting that base case to 0 makes every answer 0.

## Apply the state test: decoding digits

Suppose codes from 1 through 26 represent letters A through Z. Define one state per suffix: the number of ways to decode the digits from that position onwards. A suffix starting with zero is impossible. Otherwise a one-digit code is valid; a two-digit code is another disjoint first choice only when its value is between 10 and 26.

```formula reference
d[n] = 1
d[i] = 0   if s_i = "0"
d[i] = d[i + 1]   if s_i ≠ "0"
  and t_i = 0
d[i] = d[i + 1] + d[i + 2]
  if s_i ≠ "0" and t_i = 1
where
d[i]: the number of valid decodings of the suffix starting at position i
s_i: the digit at zero-based position i in the input
i: a suffix starting position, from zero through n; the last line applies only before n
n: the number of input digits
t_i: one when the two digits starting at i form a code from 10 through 26, otherwise zero; it is zero at the final digit
≠: not equal to
In words: the empty suffix has one decoding (the empty one). A suffix starting with zero has none. Any other suffix counts the decodings after taking one digit, plus those after taking two digits when they form a code from 10 to 26.
```

For `"106"`, the zero cannot start a code, so the only split is `"10", "6"`. For `"226"` there are three: `2 2 6`, `22 6` and `2 26`. Evaluate suffixes from the end towards the beginning so each continuation is ready. The two choices are disjoint (the first code is either one digit or two), so adding them never double-counts.

## Key takeaways
- State definitions explain exactly which subproblem a table cell represents.
- Choose min/max, sum over disjoint alternatives, or logical OR to match the question.
- Impossible states need a sentinel value that cannot beat a feasible answer.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [MIT algorithms course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/)

questions.prompt: A minimum-coins DP initialises `dp = [0] * (amount + 1)` and then sets `dp[a] = min(dp[a - c] + 1 for c in coins if c <= a)`. With coins `[2]` and amount 3, what goes wrong?

options.text: `dp[1]` has no valid coin, so `min()` of an empty sequence raises `ValueError`
options.explanation: Correct. For amount one no coin fits, so the generator is empty. Even if you guarded that and left `dp[1]` at 0, `dp[3]` would be computed as `dp[1]` plus one coin, giving 1, and would claim 3 is makeable with one coin. Impossible states need `+∞`, not 0.

options.text: It returns 2, which is correct
options.explanation: 3 can't be made from 2s at all, so no finite answer is correct; the correct result is "impossible" (usually reported as −1).

options.text: It returns 1 because 3 // 2 = 1
options.explanation: There's no division in the recurrence. The real problem is the empty `min()` at amount one and the misleading 0 sentinel value.

options.text: It loops forever
options.explanation: The loop is bounded by `amount`; the failure is a wrong sentinel value and an empty `min()`, not non-termination.

questions.workedExample:
1. In a minimisation, an impossible state must lose every comparison, so it should be `+∞`.
2. Trace with `dp = [0, 0, 0, 0]`: at amount one no coin fits, so `min(())` gets an empty sequence and raises `ValueError`.
3. Suppose you add `default=0` to dodge the error. Amount one now claims 0 coins; amount two correctly takes one 2-coin; amount three is "amount one plus one coin", so it claims 1 coin. The fake 0 has made an impossible amount look cheap.
4. Correct version: `dp = [0] + [inf] * amount` and `default=inf`. Amount one stays infinite, amount two is 1, and amount three is infinity plus one, which is still infinity, so you report −1 (impossible).

questions.prompt: A problem asks "**how many** different ways are there to...". When the recurrence considers each possible first decision, how should the subproblem results be combined?

options.text: Take the maximum
options.explanation: Max picks the single best option, which is right for optimisation problems. Counting must account for every option.

options.text: Multiply them together
options.explanation: Multiplication counts combinations of *independent* parts done together (for example left subtree × right subtree). Alternative first decisions are mutually exclusive, so they add.

options.text: Logical OR
options.explanation: OR answers "is it possible?". It loses how many ways there are.

options.text: Sum them, making sure the options are disjoint so that no arrangement is counted twice
options.explanation: Correct. Each way of solving the problem starts with exactly one first decision, so the total is the sum, over all possible first decisions, of the number of ways to finish after that decision. The disjointness requirement is where most counting bugs come from.

questions.workedExample:
1. Climbing stairs: the first move is either 1 step or 2 steps.
2. Every way to climb n stairs starts with exactly one of those, so the two groups of ways are disjoint and together cover everything.
3. Hence the count for n stairs is the count that starts with a 1-step (the ways to climb n − 1) plus the count that starts with a 2-step (the ways to climb n − 2).
4. If the options overlapped (for example, two different decisions that lead to the same final arrangement), summing would double-count.
5. Summary of combiners: optimise → min/max; count → sum (over disjoint options); decide → any/or.

questions.prompt:
Decode a digit string where `1`→A, ..., `26`→Z. `dp[i]` is the number of ways to decode `s[i:]`; a `0` can't start a code and a two-digit code must be 10–26. The correct base case is `dp[n] = 1`, where n is the length of s.

A teammate changes it to `dp[n] = 0`, reasoning that "an empty string has no decodings". What does the program now return for `s = "11106"` (whose true answer is 2)?

options.text: 1, because only the final step of each decoding is lost
options.explanation: The base case is not subtracted once; it is the seed that every count is built from. Changing it changes every entry, not just one.

options.text: 2, because the base case is only read at the very end
options.explanation: Every decoding finishes by reaching the empty suffix, so every count reads the base case, directly or through other entries.

options.text: 0, and it will return 0 for every input
options.explanation: Correct. Each count is a sum of continuations that all end at the empty suffix. With that seed at 0, the last digit's entry is 0, the entries before it add up zeros, and the answer is 0 whatever the input.

options.text: It raises `IndexError` reading past the end of the table
options.explanation: The table still has n + 1 entries and the loop reads the same positions as before. Only the stored value changed.

questions.workedExample:
1. In a counting DP, the base case says how many ways there are to finish when nothing is left. For decoding, that is exactly one way: stop.
2. Every complete decoding is a chain of choices that ends at the empty suffix. The count at any position is the sum of the counts it can step to, so ultimately it adds up one "1" per complete decoding.
3. With `dp[n] = 0`: the entry for the final digit `"6"` is `dp[n]`, which is 0. The `"06"` entry is 0 anyway (it starts with zero). Every earlier entry adds up zeros.
4. So `dp[0]` is 0, for this input and for every other input.
5. Fix: the empty remainder is one way, not zero. With `dp[n] = 1`, "11106" gives 2: `1 1 10 6` and `11 10 6`.

questions.prompt: Which are reasons to investigate your state or memoisation implementation (rather than proofs that the state is wrong)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Your recurrence needs to know what choice was made two steps ago, but that isn't in the state
options.explanation: Correct. That's an under-specified state. Whatever the recurrence needs to remember must become a parameter (as `holding` did in the stock problem).

options.text: Your memo key includes a tuple of every item chosen so far
options.explanation: A full history key can prevent reuse and create exponentially many states. Sometimes history really is needed; investigate whether a sufficient smaller summary exists before calling it wrong.

options.text: The state has two integer parameters instead of one
options.explanation: Two parameters is completely normal (LCS, edit distance, knapsack). Dimensionality isn't a smell; missing or excess information is.

options.text: The memoised and brute-force solutions disagree on small inputs
options.explanation: Correct. If the recurrence itself matches the brute force when uncached but the memoised version doesn't, an insufficient key is one possibility; cache lifetime, mutable state and implementation bugs must also be checked.

options.text: The answer is in `dp[0]` rather than `dp[n]`
options.explanation: That just means you used suffix states rather than prefix states. Both are fine.

questions.workedExample:
1. A sufficient state contains everything needed to determine the subproblem. Extra information may be inefficient without being incorrect.
2. Too little: the recurrence wants extra history (stock without `holding`). Cache hits return answers for a different situation → wrong results.
3. Too much: keys like `(i, tuple(chosen))` are almost never repeated → no reuse → exponential time.
4. A great debugging habit: write a brute force, compare on random small inputs. A mismatch introduced by caching calls for checking the key, cache lifetime, shared mutation and implementation details.
5. Number of dimensions and whether the answer is at `dp[0]` or `dp[n]` are design choices, not errors.

lessons.title: Evaluate dependencies and recover choices
lessons.summary: Finite once-per-state evaluation requires acyclic dependencies.
lessons.body:
Once the state and transitions are correct, decide when each answer becomes available and how to recover the choices behind it.

## Step 4: evaluation order

Every DP state depends on some others. For a recurrence evaluated once per state, those dependencies must form a **directed acyclic graph** (DAG): no state may depend, directly or indirectly, on itself. Bottom-up evaluation is just a topological order of that DAG. A strictly shrinking measure (a smaller index, a shorter interval, a smaller remaining budget) is the usual proof that no cycle exists.

If the dependencies do form a cycle, plain memoisation recurses forever. Cyclic equations (such as Bellman equations in decision-making under uncertainty) need different, iterative fixed-point methods such as value iteration.

- If `dp[i]` depends on larger `i`, loop `i` downwards.
- If `dp[i][j]` depends on `[i-1][j]` and `[i][j-1]`, loop rows then columns, both upwards.
- If an interval depends on shorter intervals, loop by length.

Memoisation finds the order automatically, which is why it's a good first draft.

## Step 5: answer and reconstruction

Say which state is the answer (`dp[0]`, `dp[n]`, `max(dp)`, ...). Then, if the problem wants the actual solution, either:

- **Store the choice** that achieved each state's best value, in a parallel array, and follow it from the answer state; or
- **Recompute**: walk from the answer state and, at each step, check which option reproduces the stored value.

Following stored choices takes time proportional to the number of reconstruction steps plus output construction. Rechecking alternatives can cost more: include the number of candidates examined at each step.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a route log on a long drive
> At the end of a drive, the trip computer can tell you the total distance, but not which turns you took. If you jotted down the turn at every junction, you can read the whole route back. If you didn't, you can still work it out by checking, at each junction, which road is consistent with the distances you remember.
>
> **How it maps:** the total distance is the DP value at the answer state. The jotted turns are the stored choices, followed back from the answer. Checking which road fits the remembered distances is the recompute method: at each state, find the option that reproduces the stored value.
>
> **Where it stops:** a driver only logs the junctions they actually passed. A DP stores a choice for every state, including the many that are not on the final route, because it doesn't know the route until the end.

## Choosing between prefix and suffix states

Both work for most sequence problems. Pick whichever makes the recurrence read naturally:

- **Suffix** (`f(i)` records answer for `s[i:]`): the first decision is "what do I do at i?". It matches top-down recursion well.
- **Prefix** (`dp[i]` records answer for `s[:i]`): the last decision is "what was the final piece?". It matches left-to-right loops.

## Keeping a path while saving rows

A rolling table keeps only the latest row or two, so the older rows a traceback would need are gone. Keep per-cell choices when memory permits, or do extra work to recover them. Hirschberg’s technique (1975, for longest common subsequence and alignment) computes costs forwards from the start and backwards from the end to a middle row, picks the column where the two meet on an optimal path, and recurses on the two halves. For strings of lengths m and n, it keeps O(mn) time while using only linear extra storage plus the output. One reverse rolling pass alone does not recover every choice.

## Key takeaways
- Finite once-per-state evaluation requires acyclic dependencies.
- Store winning choices or recompute them to recover a solution.
- Prefix and suffix states are both valid when their recurrences match.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [MIT algorithms course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/)
- [Hirschberg’s algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirschberg%27s_algorithm)

lessons.title: Word break with reconstruction
lessons.summary: A suffix state decides whether the rest of the string can be split.
lessons.body:
## Worked example 1: word break

> Given a string `s` and nonempty dictionary words, can `s` be split into a sequence of dictionary words? If so, return one split.

**State.** `ok[i]` is True if the suffix `s[i:]` can be split into words.

**Recurrence.** The first decision is which word starts at position i. The suffix from i can be split if some dictionary word matches exactly at i **and** the rest after that word can also be split. In Python:

```python
ok[i] = any(s.startswith(w, i)
            and ok[i + len(w)]
            for w in words)
```

**Base case.** `ok[n] = True`: the empty suffix is trivially split (into zero words).

**Order.** `ok[i]` depends on larger indices, so loop `i` from the final character index down to zero.

**Answer.** `ok[0]`. To reconstruct, store `nxt[i]`, the end of the word chosen at i.

```python
def word_break(s, words):
    # Reuse the same word collection each
    # pass.
    words = tuple(words)
    if any(not isinstance(w, str) or not w
           for w in words):
        raise ValueError("nonempty words")
    n = len(s)
    ok = [False] * (n + 1)
    nxt = [None] * (n + 1)
    # The empty suffix needs no words.
    ok[n] = True
    # Larger suffix positions are ready
    # first.
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        for w in words:
            j = i + len(w)
            # Match one word and a
            # splittable suffix.
            if s.startswith(w, i) and ok[j]:
                # Save the successful next
                # boundary.
                ok[i], nxt[i] = True, j
                break
    # No full split exists from the
    # beginning.
    if not ok[0]:
        return None
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < n:
        # Recover the stored word choice.
        out.append(s[i:nxt[i]])
        i = nxt[i]
    return out
```

Trace `s = "catsanddog"`, words `["cat", "cats", "and", "sand", "dog"]`:

```
i  suffix       ok   via
10 ""           T    base
7  "dog"        T    dog -> 10
6  "ddog"       F
4  "anddog"     T    and -> 7
3  "sanddog"    T    sand -> 7
0  "catsanddog" T    cat -> 3
```

(Positions 1, 2, 5, 8 and 9 are False.) Following `nxt[i]` from position zero gives `["cat", "sand", "dog"]`. With "cats" listed first you'd get `["cats", "and", "dog"]`; both are valid.

**Complexity.** Count states and the work per state. Let n be the string length, W the number of dictionary words and L the longest word's length. There are n + 1 states; each tries all W words, and each `startswith` check compares up to L characters. So the work is O(nWL), with O(n + W) extra memory. A 1,000-character string with 500 words of up to 10 characters needs at most about 5 million character comparisons. Brute force, by contrast, can explore exponentially many splits of a string like `"aaaa...ab"`.

## Reduce the transition work

The states are fixed; the cost per state is what you can improve. When the dictionary is large but words are short, try **lengths** instead of words: put the words in a set and, at each position, look up the substrings of length 1 to L. The number of candidates per position now depends on L, not on W.

In Python, each candidate slice is a fresh string that costs work proportional to its length to build and hash, so this is O(nL²) character work plus O(WL) to build the set. A trie (prefix tree) avoids rebuilding slices: walk it one character at a time from position i and stop when no branch continues, for O(nL) plus O(WL) to build it. These are growth estimates, not timings.

## Key takeaways
- A suffix state decides whether the rest of the string can be split.
- Nonempty words make every dependency advance to a larger index.
- Record a successful word end to reconstruct one split.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [MIT algorithms course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/)

questions.prompt: You're solving *word break* (can string `s` be split into dictionary words?). Which state stores just one Boolean per position and directly answers the decision problem?

options.text: `dp[i]` records the number of words used so far at position i
options.explanation: The count of words used isn't what the future depends on; two different routes to i with different counts face exactly the same remaining problem. It also doesn't answer the yes/no question.

options.text: `dp[w]` records whether word w appears in s
options.explanation: Whether each word appears somewhere says nothing about whether the occurrences tile the string without gaps or overlaps.

options.text: `dp[i]` records whether the suffix `s[i:]` can be split into dictionary words
options.explanation: Correct. Knowing only i is enough to solve the rest optimally, the answer is `dp[0]`, and each state depends on strictly larger indices.

options.text: `dp[i]` stores the list of all splits of `s[:i]`
options.explanation: This is valid but over-specified: storing every split can take exponential space. A boolean per position is all the decision problem needs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask what the future depends on. Once you've split `s[:i]` successfully, the remaining question is only about `s[i:]`; how you split the prefix doesn't matter.
2. So the state is just i, and the value is a Boolean: "can the suffix from i be split?"
3. Recurrence: the suffix from i can be split if some word fits exactly at i and the suffix after that word can be split too. Base case: the empty suffix (i = n, the string length) always can.
4. The answer is `dp[0]`, the whole string.
5. A good state is the *smallest* description of a subproblem that still makes the future independent of the past.

questions.prompt: Word break on a 10,000-character string with 1,000 dictionary words, each at most twenty characters long. The lesson's version tries every dictionary word at every position. Which change cuts the work most, and why?

options.text: Put the words in a set and try only the lengths 1 to 20 at each position, so the candidates per position depend on the longest word length, not the dictionary size
options.explanation: Correct. At most 20 candidates start at each position instead of 1,000 words. Each slice still costs up to 20 characters to build and hash, but the total character work is roughly a hundred times smaller here (about 2 million rather than 200 million operations) (and a trie, which avoids rebuilding slices, cuts it further).

options.text: Use memoisation instead; it is O(n) regardless of the dictionary
options.explanation: Memoisation evaluates the same states with the same transitions. Each state still has to try candidate words, so the work can't be independent of the dictionary.

options.text: Sort the words by length; that makes the loop O(n log W)
options.explanation: Sorting doesn't reduce the number of candidates tested at each position. You'd still check up to all W words.

options.text: Nothing better exists: trying every word is optimal
options.explanation: Both set lookup by length and a trie walk beat it when words are short and the dictionary is large.

questions.workedExample:
1. The states don't change: one per suffix, 10,001 in all. Only the work per state can improve.
2. Original: at each position, try all 1,000 words, each check comparing up to 20 characters. That is up to about 20,000 character comparisons per position, about 200 million in total.
3. Set version: at each position, try only the substrings of length 1 to 20. Building and hashing them costs about 1 + 2 + … + 20 = 210 character operations per position, about 2 million in total. The candidate count is now bounded by the longest word length, not the dictionary size.
4. Trie version: walk one character at a time from each position and stop when no word continues: at most 20 steps per position, about 200,000 in total, plus building the trie.
5. These are growth estimates, not timings, but the lesson is general: once the recurrence is right, the next optimisation is usually cheaper transitions, not fewer states.

lessons.title: Add a holding state for stock trading
lessons.summary: Day alone cannot describe both holding and empty-handed histories.
lessons.body:
A position-only state is useful only when the future needs no extra information. Stock trading demonstrates a small flag that changes which actions are available.

## Worked example 2: when the state needs more than an index

> You know a stock's price on each day. You may buy and sell as often as you like, holding at most one share, but after selling you must wait one day before buying again. Maximise profit.

Try `dp[i]` records best profit from day i onwards. It doesn't work: whether you can sell on day i depends on whether you're **holding** a share. The future depends on more than i, so add that to the state.

**State.** `f(i, holding)` records best profit from day i onwards, given whether we hold a share.

**Recurrence.**

- Holding: either keep it (`f(i+1, True)`) or sell (`price[i] + f(i+2, False)`; the `+2` skips the cooldown day).
- Not holding: either wait (`f(i+1, False)`) or buy (`-price[i] + f(i+1, True)`).

Selling adds the price to the profit; buying subtracts it, which is why the buy option starts with `-price[i]`. Keep whichever option gives more profit.

**Domain and base case.** Prices are nonnegative integers, and every share bought must be sold. So once the days run out, finishing empty-handed is worth 0, and finishing while still holding a share is worth negative infinity (`−∞`): a value worse than any real profit, so an unfinished trade is never chosen, even when a share was bought for 0.

```python
from functools import cache

def max_profit(prices):
    prices = tuple(prices)
    if any(type(p) is not int or p < 0
           for p in prices):
        raise ValueError("price domain")
    n = len(prices)

    # Repeated arguments reuse stored
    # answers.
    @cache
    def f(i, holding):
        # Reject a share never sold by the
        # end.
        if i >= n:
            return (-float("inf")
                    if holding else 0)
        # Waiting preserves the holding
        # state.
        skip = f(i + 1, holding)
        if holding:
            # Selling skips the following
            # cooldown day.
            sell = prices[i] + f(i+2, False)
            return max(skip, sell)
        # Buying pays now and enables later
        # sales.
        buy = -prices[i] + f(i + 1, True)
        return max(skip, buy)

    return f(0, False)
```

For prices `[1, 2, 3, 0, 2]` this returns 3. The tempting plan, buy at 1 and sell at 3 (+2), forces a cooldown on the day priced 0, leaving only one day: total 2. The better plan is buy at 1, sell at 2 (+1), cool down on the day priced 3, buy at 0, sell at 2 (+2): total 3. Spotting that by hand is fiddly, which is exactly why you let the recurrence try every option.

**Complexity.** With n days, there are about 2n states (two per day, plus the end) with O(1) arithmetic operations each, so O(n) time. The shown version keeps O(n) cached states, prices and recursion frames. An iterative hold/sold/rest version can use O(1) value slots; integer bit costs remain additional.

> [!tip] The state machine view
> Many "sequence with modes" problems are DP over (position, mode). Draw the modes as boxes and the allowed moves between them as arrows; each arrow is a term in the recurrence.

```
 rest --buy--> hold --sell--> sold
  ^ |           ^ |             |
  +-+ wait      +-+ keep        |
  ^                             |
  +-------- cooldown -----------+
```

## A transaction limit changes the state

Without a cooldown, a cap on the number of buy-sell transactions needs one more parameter: how many transactions are still allowed. Keep the holding flag too. A convenient convention is to spend one allowance when you buy; the matching sale then needs nothing extra. The state becomes (day, transactions left, holding): still a constant number of choices per state, but k + 1 times as many states for a limit of k. As before, finishing while still holding a share is forbidden.

## Pitfalls

1. **Under-specified state.** The stock problem without `holding`. Symptom: a recurrence that needs to "remember" something it can't see.
2. **Over-specified state.** Including the full path or a list in the key. It explodes the number of states and usually means you haven't found what really matters.
3. **Double counting.** In "how many ways" problems the options must be disjoint. Counting coin combinations versus orderings is the classic trap (the later unit “Count combinations or ordered sequences”).
4. **Wrong sentinel value.** Using `0` for "impossible" in a minimisation makes impossible states look free. Use `float('inf')`.
5. **Order bugs.** Bottom-up code that reads a cell before it's filled. If unsure, write it top-down first and convert.

## Key takeaways
- Day alone cannot describe both holding and empty-handed histories.
- Selling jumps over the cooldown day.
- Forbid unfinished trades with a negative-infinity terminal value.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [MIT algorithms course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/)

What information is missing?

options.text: The problem lacks overlapping subproblems
options.explanation: It has plenty of overlap: many buy/sell sequences reach the same day in the same position. The issue is that i alone doesn't identify a subproblem.

options.text: Prefix states would work, but suffix states can't
options.explanation: A prefix `dp[i]` has the same flaw: the best profit up to day i depends on whether you end the day holding a share. Direction isn't the issue.

options.text: It needs O(n²) states, so `dp[i]` is too small
options.explanation: The fix only doubles the states to 2n. It's about missing information, not size.

options.text: What you're allowed to do from day i depends on whether you currently hold a share (and whether you just sold), so i alone doesn't determine the best future
options.explanation: Correct. Two histories that both reach day i, one holding and one not, face different options. The state must include `holding` (and the cooldown is handled by jumping to i + 2 after a sale).

questions.workedExample:

2. On day 0 of `[1, 2, 3, 0, 2]`, someone already holding a share can still collect 4 (sell at 2, cool down, buy at 0, sell at 2), while someone empty-handed can make at most 3. Same day, different futures.
3. So a single `dp[0]` value cannot represent both situations. The state is under-specified.
4. Fix: `f(i, holding)`. Holding, you either keep the share or sell it and jump to day i + 2 (the cooldown). Not holding, you either wait or buy at today's price. At the end, empty-handed is worth 0 and still holding is forbidden (−∞).
5. There are about 2n states with O(1) work each, so O(n) in total.

questions.prompt: Extend the stock problem: no cooldown, but at most **k** buy-sell transactions. With 1,000 days and a limit of 100 transactions, which state and complexity fit?

options.explanation: Without the transaction count and holding flag, the state can't tell whether another buy is allowed or a sale is possible.

options.text: `f(i, transactions_left, holding)`; about 2 × 1,000 × 101 ≈ 2 × 10⁵ states with O(1) work each
options.explanation: Correct. Each extra fact the future depends on becomes a parameter: one state per day, per number of transactions left (0 to 100), per holding flag, about 200,000 in all. Each state has a constant number of choices, so the work grows with days × transaction limit.

options.text: `f(i, set of days traded)`; O(2ⁿ)
