2. With s running upwards, `cnt[s - x]` has already been updated with x in the same round. For example, while processing 5, `cnt[5]` becomes 2 ({5} and {2, 3}) before `cnt[10]` reads it, so {5, 5} gets counted.
3. The upward version counts collections in which each value may repeat: the three real subsets plus four with repeats, such as {5, 5}, {2, 2, 6}, {2, 2, 3, 3} and {2, 2, 2, 2, 2}.
4. This is the same one-character bug as 0/1 versus unbounded knapsack: the loop direction decides whether an item can be reused.

lessons.title: Split totals into equal or near-equal groups
lessons.summary: An equal partition needs an even total and a reachable half-total.
lessons.body:
Subset sum answers whether a chosen group can reach an exact total. Partition uses that answer to balance two groups without changing the input domain.

## Partition

> Can `nums` be split into two groups with equal sums?

If the total is odd, equal integer sums are impossible. Otherwise use subset sum with half the total as the target: if one group reaches exactly half, the numbers left over make up the other half automatically.

```python
def can_partition(nums):
    nums = tuple(nums)
    if any(type(x) is not int or x < 0
           for x in nums):
        raise ValueError("nonnegative nums")
    # Equal groups must each take half the
    # total.
    S = sum(nums)
    return S % 2 == 0 and \
        subset_sum(nums, S // 2)
```

For `[1, 5, 11, 5]`, the total is 22 and selecting the single 11 reaches half, so the answer is `True`. For `[1, 2, 3, 5]`, the total is odd at 11, so the answer is `False`.

**Minimum difference partition** (split into two groups as evenly as possible): compute every reachable subset sum up to half the total and take the largest one. That group is the smaller side, and the gap is the total minus twice its sum.

For `[1, 5, 11, 5]`, the reachable half-total gives difference zero. For `[1, 2, 3, 5]`, the best smaller group has sum 5 (5 alone, or 2 plus 3); the other group has sum 6, so the difference is 1.

## Key takeaways
- An equal partition needs an even total and a reachable half-total.
- The largest reachable sum at most half the total gives the smallest gap.

## Further reading
- [Knapsack recurrences](https://cp-algorithms.com/dynamic_programming/knapsack.html)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

questions.prompt: How do you reduce the **partition problem** ("split `nums` into two groups with equal sums") to subset sum?

options.text: Run subset sum with target `max(nums)`
options.explanation: The largest element has nothing to do with the target. Each group must sum to half the total.

options.text: If the total S is odd, answer False; otherwise run subset sum with target S / 2
options.explanation: Correct. If some subset sums to half the total, the numbers left over sum to the other half. An odd total can't be halved into integers.

options.text: Sort the array and check whether the first half sums to the second half
options.explanation: Groups don't have to be the first and second halves of the sorted array. [1, 5, 11, 5] partitions as {11} and {1, 5, 5}.

options.text: Run subset sum with target S
options.explanation: The whole array always sums to S. That tells you nothing about splitting.

The work grows with the numeric total, not just the number of items.

lessons.title: Numeric value versus encoded input size
lessons.summary: A numeric capacity can be exponentially larger than its bit length.
lessons.body:
## Pseudo-polynomial time

0/1 knapsack takes O(n · W) time, where n is the number of items and W the weight limit. That looks polynomial. It isn't, quite.

Complexity is measured against the **size of the input**: the number of bits needed to write it. The input includes every weight and value as well as W, so their bit lengths all matter. Writing W in binary takes far fewer bits than W itself: one thousand needs only ten binary digits, yet the table needs 1,001 columns.

```formula reference
b = ⌊log_2(W)⌋ + 1
W < 2^b
T = O(nW)
T = O(n × 2^b)
where
b: the number of bits needed to write W in binary
W: the capacity, a positive whole number
log_2(W): the base-2 logarithm of W, the power you raise 2 to in order to get W
⌊x⌋: floor, x rounded down to a whole number
2^b: b copies of 2 multiplied together
T: the running time of the table algorithm
n: the number of items
O(...): Big-O, growing at most in proportion to the expression inside
In words: W is about 2 to the power of its bit length, so work proportional to W is exponential in the number of bits used to write it.
```

The capacity-based bound is therefore not polynomial in the full binary encoding length.

| Capacity | Bits | Work proxy: 100 items |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 10 | 100,000 |
| 1,000,000 | 20 | 100,000,000 |
| 1,000,000,000 | 30 | 100 billion |
| 10¹⁸ | 60 | 10²⁰ |

Adding ten bits to W multiplies the work by about 1,000 (2¹⁰ = 1,024). An algorithm that's polynomial in the **numeric value** but not in its bit length is called **pseudo-polynomial**.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: tally marks versus digits
> Writing "1,000,000" takes seven digits, but counting it out in tally marks takes a million strokes. Adding one more digit to the number makes the tally ten times longer.
>
> **How it maps:** the input to an algorithm is the written number, so its size is the number of digits (bits, in binary). A capacity-indexed DP makes one column of its table for every unit of capacity, like drawing every tally mark. Its work grows with the number's value, which is exponential in the number of digits used to write it.
>
> **Where it stops:** computers write numbers in binary, so each extra bit doubles the value rather than multiplying it by ten. And unlike a tally, the DP's cost also multiplies by the number of items, and many practical instances have small enough capacities that it runs quickly.

This is consistent with knapsack, subset sum and partition being **NP-complete** (as decision problems). These decision versions are **weakly NP-complete**: they have pseudo-polynomial algorithms, unlike strongly NP-complete numeric problems, unless every problem whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time, a statement widely believed to be false. Large numbers do not make every individual instance difficult. When the numbers are small (bounded by a polynomial in n), DP solves them efficiently. Contrast with *strongly* NP-hard problems like the travelling salesman, whose decision versions remain NP-complete even with polynomially bounded weights.

## Key takeaways
- A numeric capacity can be exponentially larger than its bit length.
- Capacity-indexed DP is pseudo-polynomial.
- Small numeric bounds can make weakly NP-complete problems manageable.

## Further reading
- [Knapsack recurrences](https://cp-algorithms.com/dynamic_programming/knapsack.html)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

questions.prompt: Subset sum is NP-complete, yet for n numbers and target T there's an O(n·T) DP for it. Why doesn't this prove that every problem whose answers can be checked in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time?

options.text: Because the DP is only correct for positive integers
options.explanation: The DP's restriction to non-negative integers isn't the reason; the NP-complete version also uses non-negative integers.

options.text: Because O(n·T) is polynomial only in the numeric value of T, which can be exponential in the number of bits used to write T; in terms of input size the DP is exponential
options.explanation: Correct. A 64-bit T can be about 1.8 × 10¹⁹, so the table would be astronomically large. Polynomial in the input length would have to be polynomial in log T (the number of bits of T).

options.text: Because the DP uses too much memory, and P only counts time
options.explanation: Memory isn't the issue: the DP's *time* is exponential in input size too.

options.text: Because the DP only decides feasibility and doesn't find the subset
options.explanation: Reconstruction from the DP table is easy, and NP-completeness is about the decision problem anyway.

questions.workedExample:
1. Complexity classes measure time against input length in bits.
2. Input: n numbers and T. Writing T takes only about log₂ T bits, and T is less than 2 to the power of that bit count. So time proportional to T is exponential in the number of bits used to write it.
3. Example: a 30-bit target (about 10⁹) with one hundred items needs about 10¹¹ table cells. A 60-bit target needs about 10²⁰.
4. Such an algorithm is pseudo-polynomial. Subset sum is also NP-complete, so this is a weakly NP-complete example. Having a pseudo-polynomial algorithm alone does not make an arbitrary problem NP-hard; large-valued individual instances can still be easy.

lessons.title: Alternative strategies for huge capacities
lessons.summary: Small total values suggest indexing by value instead of weight.
lessons.body:
A weight-indexed table can be too large even for a modest item count. Choose a different state or a different guarantee according to which quantity is small.

### What to do when W is huge

- **DP over value instead of weight**: `minW[v]` records minimum weight needed to achieve value exactly v. It takes O(n · V) time, where V is the total of all values. Useful when values are small but weights are big.
- **Meet in the middle**: for n up to about 40, split the items in half and list every subset of each half: only about a million per half for forty items. Sort one half by weight, record the best value seen so far at each position of that sorted list, and, for each subset of the other half, binary-search for the heaviest partner that still fits and read off that best value. That is a few tens of millions of steps (about twenty million comparisons for the searches, plus a sort of similar size) instead of about 1.1 trillion subsets for full enumeration, and the work does not depend on W at all (ignoring the cost of arithmetic on very large numbers).

- **Approximation algorithms**: scale and round the values, then run the value DP. Pick an allowed relative error ε (epsilon) between 0 and 1. For nonnegative values, discard individually overweight items, choose an appropriate scaling factor and handle the zero-optimum case separately. The appropriately scaled value DP has the following guarantee:

```formula reference
A ≥ (1 − ε)OPT
0 < ε < 1
where
A: the value obtained by the approximation algorithm
OPT: the largest feasible total value
ε: epsilon, the chosen relative-error tolerance
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: The returned value loses at most the chosen fraction of the optimum.
```

For a one-percent tolerance the returned value is at least 99 percent of the optimum. With n items, its work is polynomial in n and the reciprocal of the tolerance, plus input bit costs: an FPTAS. The correct scaling construction is required; arbitrary rounding does not establish this guarantee.
- **Branch and bound / integer programming** solvers can exploit structure in some large instances, but retain exponential worst-case risks.

## Key takeaways
- Small total values suggest indexing by value instead of weight.
- Meet in the middle reduces dependence on the item count.
- Approximation and exact solvers have different guarantees.

## Further reading
- [Knapsack recurrences](https://cp-algorithms.com/dynamic_programming/knapsack.html)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

questions.prompt: 0/1 knapsack with forty items whose weights are up to 10¹², and a weight limit of five trillion. Values are also large. What's a practical exact approach?

options.text: The standard O(n·W) DP
options.explanation: The nW work expression is 2 × 10¹⁴. A full table uses about that many entries, while a rolling row still needs W + 1 ≈ 5 × 10¹² entries. These require substantial resources.

options.text: Meet in the middle: enumerate the 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶ subsets of each half, sort one half by weight (keeping a running max value), and for each subset of the other half binary-search the best partner
options.explanation: Correct. About 2 × 10⁶ subsets plus sorting and binary searches: ~10⁶ × 20 operations, independent of W’s numeric value in the unit-cost model; operand bit costs remain.

options.text: DP over value: `minW[v]`
options.explanation: That's O(n · total value). With large values it's just as infeasible as DP over weight.

options.text: Brute force all 2⁴⁰ subsets
options.explanation: Enumerating all forty-item subsets requires about 1.1 trillion candidates. Meet in the middle reduces the enumerated sets to roughly two million before sorting and searching; actual runtime depends on implementation and resources.

questions.workedExample:
1. Both the weight DP and the value DP are pseudo-polynomial; with 10¹²-scale numbers neither works.
2. Forty items is modest, so think exponential-in-n, but halve the exponent.
3. Split into halves L and R of 20 items. Enumerate all (weight, value) pairs for each: 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 each.
4. Sort R by weight; replace each value with the max value seen so far (prefix max), and drop dominated pairs.
5. For each left subset that fits, binary-search the sorted right half for the heaviest weight that still fits in the space left, and read the best value up to that point from the running maximum. The best total over all left subsets is the answer.
6. About a million left subsets times about 20 binary-search steps: roughly twenty million steps, plus the sorting. None of it depends on how large W is, only on the number of items (and on arithmetic with large integers).

lessons.title: Recognise budgets and signed-sum reductions
lessons.summary: A subset choice under an additive budget often has a knapsack state.
lessons.body:
## Recognising knapsack

Ask: "Am I choosing a **subset** of items, subject to a **budget** on some additive quantity, while optimising or counting another additive quantity?" If so, the state is (items considered, budget used), and it's knapsack. Examples:

- **Target sum** ("assign + or − to each number to reach T"): it turns into subset counting for nonnegative integer inputs. The numbers given a plus sign form one group; everything else is subtracted. Fixing the plus group's sum fixes the whole expression, so the plus group must sum to exactly half of (the total + the target):

```formula reference
P − (S − P) = T
P = (S + T) / 2
where
P: the sum of the numbers given a + sign
S: the sum of all the numbers
S − P: the sum of the numbers given a − sign
T: the target the signed numbers must add up to
In words: the plus group's sum minus the minus group's sum must equal the target, which fixes the plus group's sum at half of (the total of all the numbers + the target), so count the subsets with that sum.
```

For five ones with target three, the plus group must sum to 4: count the subsets of sum 4, of which there are 5 (choose which four 1s are positive). Equal-valued positions still count as distinct.

Two checks come first. If the target is further from zero than the total, no assignment can reach it. And if the total plus the target is odd, the plus group would need a fractional sum, so no assignment exists. Skipping that parity check is a real bug: integer division silently rounds the half down, and the code counts subsets for the wrong target.

- **Last stone weight II**: minimum-difference partition.
- **Ones and zeroes**: knapsack with a two-dimensional budget (count of 0s and 1s), state `dp[zeros][ones]`.

## Key takeaways
- A subset choice under an additive budget often has a knapsack state.
- Target sum becomes subset counting with a parity and range check.
- Equal-valued input positions remain distinct choices.

## Further reading
- [Knapsack recurrences](https://cp-algorithms.com/dynamic_programming/knapsack.html)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

questions.prompt: *Target sum*: count the ways to assign `+` or `−` to each number so the expression equals T. A teammate reduces it to subset counting with `P = (S + T) // 2`, where S is the sum of the numbers, and returns the number of subsets that sum to P. For `nums = [1, 1, 1, 1]` and `T = 1` it returns 6. What is wrong?

options.text: It is missing the parity check: S + T = 5 is odd, so no assignment exists and the answer should be 0
options.explanation: Correct. The plus group would need a sum of 2.5. Floor division rounds it down to 2, and the code counts the 6 subsets that sum to 2, which correspond to expressions equal to 0, not 1.

options.text: It is missing the range check: the target is larger than the total
options.explanation: The target 1 is well within the total 4. The range check passes; the parity check is the one that fails.

options.text: Nothing: there really are 6 ways, one for each pair of plus signs
options.explanation: Two plus signs and two minus signs give 1 + 1 − 1 − 1 = 0, not 1. With four ±1 terms the result is always even, so 1 is unreachable.

options.text: It counts the empty subset, which should be excluded
options.explanation: The empty subset has sum 0, so it is never counted for P = 2. And in general the empty plus group is a legitimate assignment (all minus signs).

questions.workedExample:
1. Split the numbers into a plus group with sum P and a minus group with sum S − P. The expression equals P − (S − P), so P must equal half of S + T.
2. Here S = 4 and T = 1, so the plus group would need a sum of 2.5. No group of whole numbers has a fractional sum, so the answer is 0. You can also see it directly: four terms of ±1 always add up to an even number.
3. `(4 + 1) // 2` is 2, so the code silently counts the subsets with sum 2. There are 6 (choose which two 1s are positive), but each of them gives 1 + 1 − 1 − 1 = 0.
4. The fix: return 0 when S + T is odd or when the target is further from zero than S, and only then count subsets with sum (S + T) / 2.
5. With valid input, for example five 1s and T = 3, the plus group needs sum 4: there are 5 such subsets, one for each choice of the single minus sign.

questions.prompt: Which of these are correctly modelled as a knapsack-style DP over (items, budget)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Split `[1, 6, 11, 5]` into two groups minimising the difference of their sums (answer: 1)
options.explanation: Correct. The total is 23, so look for reachable subset sums up to half of it, 11.5, so at most 11. The largest is 11, leaving 12 for the other group: a difference of 1.

options.text: Choose binary strings from a list to maximise how many you take, using at most m zeros and n ones in total
options.explanation: Correct. 0/1 knapsack with a two-dimensional budget: state `dp[z][o]`, iterate both dimensions downwards for each string.

options.text: Find the shortest path between two cities in a road network
options.explanation: There's no subset-under-a-budget structure. That's a graph shortest-path problem (Dijkstra, or DP over a DAG if acyclic).

options.text: Choose features for a release to maximise customer value, assuming independent features, additive values, integer engineering-day costs and one 60-day budget
options.explanation: Correct. Under the stated independence and additive-cost assumptions, features are 0/1 items and engineering days are the budget. Dependencies or multiple people/resources would require a richer model.

options.text: Sort an array
options.explanation: Sorting isn't choosing a subset under a budget; there's no knapsack structure.

questions.workedExample:
Knapsack test: choose a subset, subject to an additive budget, optimising or counting another additive quantity.

1. Min-difference partition: subset of numbers, budget half the total, maximise sum. For [1, 6, 11, 5] the total is 23, and 11 is reachable (11 alone, or 6 + 5). One group gets 11 and the other 12: a difference of 1.

2. Ones and zeroes: subset of strings, two budgets (zeros, ones), maximise count. The budget, and so the state, is 2-D.
3. Shortest path: no subset/budget, so no.
4. Release planning: subset of features, 60-day budget, maximise value. Yes.
5. Sorting: no.

lessons.title: Intervals, split points and cubic work
lessons.summary: Interval dependencies are smaller ranges.
lessons.body:
So far every state has been a prefix, a suffix or a pair of prefixes. Two more shapes cover a large class of harder problems:

- **Interval DP**: the state is an unbroken range `[i, j]`, and the recurrence splits it at some point k.
- **Tree DP**: the state is a node (often with a small flag), and the answer combines the answers of its children.

## Interval DP: the pattern

```formula reference
dp[i][j] = best of g(dp[i][k], dp[k + 1][j],
  cost(i, k, j))   for i ≤ k < j
where
dp[i][j]: the answer for the unbroken range of elements i to j, inclusive
i, j: the first and last positions of the range, 0 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n − 1
k: the split point: the left part is i to k and the right part is k + 1 to j
best: min or max, whichever the problem asks for, taken over every split point k
g: the problem's rule for combining the two parts' answers with the cost of joining them (often just adding them)
cost(i, k, j): the cost of the final step that joins the two parts
n: the number of elements in the whole sequence
In words: try every place to split the range, combine the best answers for the two pieces, and keep the best split.
```

- **States**: O(n²) intervals, for n sequence elements.
- **Transitions**: O(n) split points each.
- **Total**: usually **O(n³)** time and O(n²) slots. The exact count is smaller than n³: for matrix chain it is about n³/6 split candidates, roughly 21 million for 500 matrices. Cubic growth means doubling n multiplies the work by about 8.
- **Order**: every interval depends on strictly shorter ones, so loop by **length**, from short to long.

## Recognise the interval boundary

For an optimal search tree over sorted keys, the chosen root divides a key interval into the ranges on its left and right. CYK parsing splits a substring and combines two grammar symbols allowed by a rule. Cutting a rod at fixed marks chooses a first cut inside a piece; the two resulting marked intervals are independent, and that cut costs the original piece’s length. These have range states and split choices. LIS ending states and ordinary tree include/exclude states have different dependency shapes.

## Key takeaways
- Interval dependencies are smaller ranges.
- Increasing interval length is a valid evaluation order.
- Count all split candidates rather than equating a cubic bound with an exact count.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [Matrix chain multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_chain_multiplication)

questions.prompt: In an interval DP over a sequence of n elements, where `dp[i][j]` is computed from `dp[i][k]` and `dp[k+1][j]` for `i ≤ k < j`, which evaluation order is always valid?

options.text: Row by row, i from 0 up to n−1, j from i up to n−1
options.explanation: With i increasing, `dp[k+1][j]` (a later row) isn't ready when you compute row i.

options.text: Any order, as long as the base cases are set
options.explanation: Interior cells depend on other interior cells. Reading one before it's computed gives a wrong value.

options.text: By increasing interval length `j - i`
options.explanation: Correct. Both `[i, k]` and `[k+1, j]` are strictly shorter than `[i, j]`, so all of them are done before any interval of the current length.

options.text: By decreasing interval length
options.explanation: That computes long intervals first, before the short sub-intervals they depend on.

questions.workedExample:
1. Dependencies of `[i, j]`: the left part `[i, k]` stops before j, and the right part `[k+1, j]` starts after i, because the split k is at least i and less than j. So both parts are strictly shorter than the whole interval.

2. So length strictly decreases along every dependency: process lengths 1, 2, ..., n.
3. Loop over lengths with `range(2, n + 1)`. For each length, visit starts using `range(n - length + 1)` and compute the endpoint with `j = i + length - 1`.
4. Row-wise with i *descending* and j ascending also works, but length order is the one that's valid when every dependency is a strictly shorter interval.

questions.prompt: A matrix chain DP (O(n²) intervals, up to n split points each) takes 2 seconds for a chain of 500 matrices. Roughly how long should you expect it to take for 1,000 matrices on the same machine?

options.text: About 4 seconds, because the work grows with the number of matrices
options.explanation: That would be linear growth. Both the number of intervals and the splits per interval grow with n.

options.text: About 8 seconds, because the number of table cells quadruples
options.explanation: The table does quadruple, but each cell also tries about twice as many split points.

options.text: About 16 seconds, because cubic work multiplies by 2³ = 8 when n doubles
options.explanation: Correct. The split-candidate count is about n³/6: roughly 21 million for 500 matrices and 167 million for 1,000, eight times as many. Timing extrapolation like this is approximate, but the factor of 8 is the signature of cubic work.

options.text: Far longer than a minute, because the number of bracketings grows exponentially
options.explanation: The number of possible bracketings (a Catalan number) does explode, but the DP never enumerates them. It only tries split points for each interval.

questions.workedExample:
1. Count the work: about n²/2 intervals, each trying up to n − 1 split points. In total about n³/6 split candidates.
2. For 500 matrices that is about 21 million; for 1,000 it is about 167 million: eight times as many.
3. So if 500 matrices took 2 seconds, expect roughly 16 seconds for 1,000, assuming the time is dominated by the inner loop. Real timings also depend on memory effects and integer sizes, so treat this as an estimate.
4. The general habit: identify the growth rate, then scale. Doubling n doubles linear work, quadruples quadratic work and multiplies cubic work by 8.

questions.prompt: For each problem, would the natural DP state be an interval `[i, j]` that is split at some k? Select all that apply.

options.text: Given access frequencies for sorted keys, build the binary search tree with the minimum expected search cost
options.explanation: Correct. Choosing the root k of keys i..j splits them into the left subtree (i..k−1) and right subtree (k+1..j): textbook interval DP, O(n³) for n keys, or O(n²) with Knuth's optimisation.

options.text: Decide whether a string can be generated by a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form
options.explanation: Correct. That's CYK: for each substring [i, j] and each split point, check whether a rule A → BC (symbol A can be rewritten as B followed by C) has B generating [i, k] and C generating [k+1, j].

options.text: Find the longest increasing subsequence
options.explanation: LIS uses a 1-D state ("ending at i"); nothing is gained by considering arbitrary intervals and splitting them.

options.text: Find the cheapest way to cut a rod at a set of marked positions, where each cut costs the current piece's length
options.explanation: Correct. The state is the piece between two marks, and the first cut in it splits it into two independent pieces. (Unlike burst balloons, choosing the first action works here: the first cut in a piece costs that piece's length whichever mark is chosen, and the two resulting pieces never interact.)

options.text: Maximum independent set in a tree
options.explanation: That's tree DP: states are nodes (with an include/exclude flag), and subproblems are subtrees, not ranges of consecutive positions.

questions.workedExample:
The interval DP signature: the answer for an unbroken range depends on choosing a split point k inside it, and the two sides are then independent.

1. Optimal BST: root k splits keys into two ranges. Yes.
2. CYK: a rule A → BC splits the substring at k. Yes.
3. LIS: the subproblem is a prefix ending at i. No.
4. Rod cutting with marks: cutting at mark k splits the piece between marks i and j into two independent pieces, and the cut costs the current length of the piece, whichever mark inside it is chosen. Yes, O(m³) for m marks.
5. Tree MIS: subtrees, not ranges. No.

lessons.title: Why matrix multiplication order matters
lessons.summary: Exact matrix multiplication is associative, but evaluation costs differ.
lessons.body:
## Matrix chain multiplication

With the classical dense algorithm, multiplying a matrix with 10 rows and 30 columns by one with 30 rows and 5 columns takes 10 × 30 × 5 = 1,500 scalar multiplications (multiplications of single numbers): the result has 10 × 5 entries, and each is a sum of 30 products. In general the cost is the three dimensions multiplied together: rows of the first, the shared inner dimension, and columns of the second.

```formula reference
cost = pqr
where
cost: the number of scalar multiplications
p: the number of rows of the first matrix
q: the number of columns of the first matrix, which must equal the number of rows of the second
r: the number of columns of the second matrix
In words: the cost is the first matrix's row count × the shared inner dimension × the second matrix's column count, because the result has one entry per row–column pair and each entry is a sum of one product per position along the shared dimension.
```

Matrix multiplication is associative in exact arithmetic, so for a chain A·B·C you can choose the bracketing, and the costs can differ wildly.

With A: 10 × 30, B: 30 × 5, C: 5 × 60:

- **(AB)C**: AB costs 1,500 and leaves a small 10 × 5 matrix; multiplying that by C costs 3,000. Total 4,500.
- **A(BC)**: BC costs 9,000 and leaves a bigger 30 × 60 matrix; multiplying A by it costs 18,000. Total 27,000.

Same answer, six times as many scalar multiplications in this cost model, just from the brackets. The difference comes from the sizes of the intermediate results: a bracketing that creates a large intermediate matrix pays for it twice, once to build it and again to use it. "Associative" means the result doesn't depend on the brackets; it says nothing about the cost. The number of possible bracketings of a chain of n matrices is the (n − 1)th Catalan number, which grows exponentially (about 4ⁿ, divided by a polynomial in n): 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, ... for chain lengths one, two, three and onwards, and 1,430 already for 9 matrices. So trying them all is out.

## Key takeaways
- Exact matrix multiplication is associative, but evaluation costs differ.
- The classical dense model counts multiplications of individual numbers.
- Choose brackets without changing the exact result.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [Matrix chain multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_chain_multiplication)

questions.prompt: Matrices A: 10 × 20, B: 20 × 30, C: 30 × 40. Using the classical dense cost model (multiplying a p × q matrix by a q × r matrix costs p·q·r scalar multiplications), which bracketing of A·B·C is cheaper, and why?

options.text: A(BC), because C is the largest matrix and should be dealt with first
options.explanation: Multiplying B and C first builds a 20 × 40 intermediate, costing 24,000, and then 8,000 more: 32,000 in all. Handling the biggest matrix first is not a reliable rule.

options.text: (AB)C, because its intermediate result is a small 10 × 30 matrix: 18,000 scalar multiplications against 32,000
options.explanation: Correct. AB costs 6,000 and keeps A's small row count of 10; multiplying that by C costs 12,000. A(BC) builds a larger intermediate and pays 32,000.

options.text: Both cost the same, because matrix multiplication is associative
options.explanation: Being associative guarantees the same *result*, not the same cost. The bracketing changes the sizes of the intermediate matrices and so the work.

options.text: Neither: every bracketing multiplies all four dimensions together, 240,000
options.explanation: Each single multiplication costs three dimensions multiplied together, not four. 10·20·30·40 is not the cost of any bracketing.

questions.workedExample:
1. One multiplication of a p × q matrix by a q × r matrix costs p·q·r: the result has p × r entries, each a sum of q products.
2. (AB)C: AB costs 10·20·30 = 6,000 and gives a 10 × 30 matrix. Multiplying that by C costs 10·30·40 = 12,000. Total 18,000.
3. A(BC): BC costs 20·30·40 = 24,000 and gives a 20 × 40 matrix. Multiplying A by it costs 10·20·40 = 8,000. Total 32,000.
4. (AB)C wins because its intermediate stays small. For longer chains no simple rule of thumb is safe, which is why the DP tries every last split k.

lessons.title: Build the matrix-chain cost table
lessons.summary: The final multiplication defines two independent subchains.
lessons.body:
The previous unit counted the scalar multiplications for a particular bracketing. Now minimise that count across every bracketing without enumerating them all.

Represent the chain by a dimension list `p`: each matrix’s row count is its entry in the list, and its column count is the following entry. Neighbouring matrices therefore share their inner dimension.

**State**: `C[i][j]` records minimum cost to multiply matrices i through j.

**Recurrence**: the **last** multiplication splits the chain into `(i..k)` and `(k+1..j)`. The left product’s rows come from the first matrix and its columns from the split. The right product shares that inner dimension and ends with the final matrix’s column count. The final cost is their three dimensions multiplied together:

```formula essential
C[i][j] = min(C[i][k] + C[k + 1][j]
  + p_i p_{k+1} p_{j+1})   for i ≤ k < j
C[i][i] = 0
where
C[i][j]: the fewest scalar multiplications needed to multiply matrices i to j (counting from 0)
i, j: the first and last matrix in the sub-chain
k: the split point: the last multiplication joins product i..k with product k+1..j
p_i: the number of rows of matrix i (p[i] in the code); matrix i is p_i × p_{i+1}
p_{k+1}: the columns of matrix k, which equal the rows of matrix k + 1
p_{j+1}: the number of columns of matrix j
min: the smallest value over every split point k
In words: try every place for the last multiplication, add the best costs of the two halves to the cost of that final multiply, and keep the cheapest.
```

A single matrix needs no multiplications. For the dimensions `[10, 30, 5, 60]`, the final multiplication can come after the first matrix (cost 27,000 in total) or after the second (4,500), so `C[0][2]` is 4,500.

```python
def matrix_chain(p):
    p = tuple(p)
    if not p or any(type(x) is not int
                    or x <= 0 for x in p):
        raise ValueError("positive dims")
    n = len(p) - 1
    # An empty chain needs no products.
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    C = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    # Shorter subchains are complete first.
    for length in range(2, n + 1):
        for i in range(n - length + 1):
            j = i + length - 1
            # Try every position of the
            # final split.
            C[i][j] = min(
                C[i][k] + C[k+1][j]
                + p[i] * p[k+1] * p[j+1]
                for k in range(i, j))
    return C[0][n - 1]
```

`matrix_chain([10, 30, 5, 60])` returns 4,500. For `[40, 20, 30, 10, 30]` (four matrices) it returns 26,000, via `((A(BC))D)`. Store the best k in a parallel `split` table to print the bracketing recursively.

The table fills diagonal by diagonal:

```
         j=0   j=1   j=2
 i=0      0   1500  4500
 i=1            0   9000
 i=2                  0
```

> [!note] Where this matters
> Numerical libraries face this directly. `numpy.linalg.multi_dot` chooses an optimal multiplication order for a chain of arrays; its source follows the textbook matrix-chain DP (three arrays use a direct cost comparison). `numpy.einsum` with `optimize=True` uses a greedy contraction-order search, which need not find the global optimum. Database query optimisers solve a harder cousin when ordering joins.

## Key takeaways
- The final multiplication defines two independent subchains.
- Keep the cheapest split and optionally store it for reconstruction.
- A single matrix has zero multiplication cost.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [Matrix chain multiplication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_chain_multiplication)
- [NumPy multi_dot](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.multi_dot.html)
- [NumPy einsum](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.einsum.html)

lessons.title: Burst balloons by choosing the last move
lessons.summary: An early burst changes the adjacency of the remaining pieces.
lessons.body:
## Burst balloons: think about the last move

> Balloons in a row have numbers. Bursting balloon k earns the product of its value and both neighbours’ values, where left and right are its *current* neighbours (or 1 past the ends). Maximise total coins.

The obvious state, "which balloon do I burst **first** in `[i, j]`?", fails: after bursting it, its neighbours become adjacent, so the two halves aren't independent.

The trick is to ask which balloon is burst **last** in an open interval `(i, j)`. The subproblem keeps boundary balloons i and j present. If k is last, then when it is burst its neighbours are exactly i and j (everything between has gone). And the balloons in `(i, k)` and `(k, j)` never interact with each other, because k stands between them the whole time.

Pad the array with 1s at both ends: `a = [1] + nums + [1]`.

```formula essential
B[i][j] = max(B[i][k] + B[k][j]
  + a_i a_k a_j)   for i < k < j
B[i][i + 1] = 0
where
B[i][j]: the most coins obtainable by bursting every balloon strictly between positions i and j, with i and j still present
a_k: the number on balloon k in the padded array a (a[k] in code), whose two ends are 1
a_i, a_j: the numbers on the two boundary balloons i and j
i, j: the boundary positions, kept unburst
k: the balloon burst last between i and j
max: the largest value over every choice of k
In words: choose which balloon goes last; at that moment its neighbours are the two boundaries, and the balloons on each side were burst independently before it.
```

The base case says there is nothing to burst when no balloons lie strictly between i and j.

For `[3, 1, 5, 8]` the answer is **167**: burst 1 (3·1·5 = 15), then 5 (3·5·8 = 120), then 3 (1·3·8 = 24), then 8 (1·8·1 = 8).

> [!tip] First vs last
> When a choice changes the neighbours of what's left, try defining the recurrence by the **last** action in the interval instead of the first. The last action sees a fixed boundary; the first one doesn't.

## Key takeaways
- An early burst changes the adjacency of the remaining pieces.
- Choosing the last burst fixes both boundary neighbours.
- Two open subintervals can then be solved independently.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [MIT algorithms course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/)

15 is just the first burst. All three balloons are eventually burst and all three payouts count.
45 would need, e.g., two bursts worth 15 and one worth 15; the third burst is always the last balloon alone, worth at most 1·5·1 = 5.

3. Value 3 last: the right side (1, 5) can earn 30 (burst 1 for 3·1·5 = 15, then 5 for 3·5·1 = 15), and the last burst pays 3: total 33. Value 1 last: the two sides earn 3 and 5 and the last burst pays 1: total 9. Value 5 last: the left side (3, 1) earns 30 and the last burst pays 5: total 35.

questions.prompt: For n balloons, padded with a 1 at each end so that a[k] is the number at position k, why does burst balloons use "which balloon is burst **last** in `(i, j)`" rather than "first"? Select all that apply.

options.text: In a subproblem that keeps boundary balloons i and j present, if k is last in (i, j), its neighbours are exactly i and j, so its payout `a[i] * a[k] * a[j]` is known
options.explanation: Correct. Everything strictly between i and j has gone before k, so i and j are its neighbours. The cost is fixed by the state.

options.text: If k is last, the balloons in (i, k) and (k, j) never become neighbours of each other, so the two sides are independent subproblems
options.explanation: Correct. k stays in place as a wall until the very end, so left-side bursts never see right-side balloons. That independence is what lets the DP add the two halves.

options.text: If k is burst first, its neighbours become adjacent, so the remaining left and right parts interact
options.explanation: Correct. That interaction is why a "first burst" recurrence can't split into independent halves.

options.text: "Last" gives O(n²) instead of O(n³)
options.explanation: Both formulations would be O(n³) with n² intervals and n choices; the "first" version simply doesn't give a correct decomposition.

questions.workedExample:

2. Good idea: k is last in open interval (i, j). Before it goes, (i, k) and (k, j) are cleared separately, each bounded by k, which is still present.
3. When k finally bursts, its neighbours are i and j. The payout is the product of those three balloons’ numbers.
4. Cost: about n² intervals (for n balloons), each trying up to n choices of last balloon, so O(n³) either way. "Last" doesn't make it faster; it makes the decomposition correct.

lessons.title: Count contiguous palindromes
lessons.summary: Matching ends enclose a smaller palindrome.
lessons.body:
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. First require an unbroken range; the next unit will allow gaps between retained characters.

### Counting palindromic substrings

`P[i][j]` records True if `s[i..j]` (characters i to j inclusive) is a palindrome, a string that reads the same backwards. It is exactly when the ends match and the inside `s[i+1..j-1]` is a palindrome, or there is no inside (the range has one or two characters):

```python
def count_palindromes(s):
    n = len(s)
    P = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
    count = 0
    # Larger starting indices are ready
    # first.
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        for j in range(i, n):
            # Singletons and pairs need no
            # inner read.
            inner = j - i < 2 or P[i+1][j-1]
            if s[i] == s[j] and inner:
                P[i][j] = True
                # Count this occurrence,
                # including repeats.
                count += 1
    return count
```

`"aaa"` has 6 (three `a`s, two `aa`s, one `aaa`); `"abc"` has 3; `"racecar"` has 10. For a string of n characters this is O(n²) time and space.

Note the loop order: `i` descending, `j` ascending, because `P[i][j]` reads `P[i+1][j-1]` (next row down). Looping by length works too. Looping `i` upwards is a silent bug: the inner cell hasn't been filled yet, still reads False, and every palindrome longer than two characters is missed.

**Expand around centre** gets the same O(n²) time in O(1) space. A palindrome is centred either on a character (odd length) or on the gap between two characters (even length), so a string of n characters has 2n − 1 possible centres. For each one, grow outwards while the ends match. **Manacher's algorithm** computes a compact array of palindrome radii in O(n), reusing mirror information. That suffices to find a longest palindrome or count occurrences; explicitly listing all occurrences can require Θ(n²) output.

## Key takeaways
- Matching ends enclose a smaller palindrome.
- Single characters and matching pairs are base cases.
- Compact palindrome radii can be linear-sized even when occurrences are quadratic.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [Longest palindromic substring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longest_palindromic_substring)

questions.prompt: The correct `count_palindromes("abba")` returns 6. A teammate changes the outer loop to `for i in range(n)` (ascending), keeping `j` ascending. What does their version return, and why?

options.text: 4, because it no longer counts the pair "bb"
options.explanation: Pairs need no inner read (`j - i < 2`), so "bb" is still found. Only longer palindromes depend on an inner cell.

options.text: 6, because the loop order doesn't change which cells are True
options.explanation: Order matters here: `P[0][3]` reads `P[1][2]`, a cell in a row the ascending loop hasn't reached yet.

options.text: 10, because every substring is now treated as a palindrome
options.explanation: The table starts all False, so unfilled cells make the code miss palindromes, not invent them.

options.text: 5, because "abba" reads the inner cell for "bb" before it has been computed, sees False and is missed
options.explanation: Correct. With i ascending, row 0 is filled before row 1, so `P[1][2]` is still False when `P[0][3]` needs it. The four single letters and "bb" are still counted.

questions.workedExample:
1. `P[i][j]` depends on `P[i+1][j-1]`, the cell for the inside of the range, which lives in the **next** row.
2. The correct loop fills rows from the bottom (i descending), so the inside is always ready. The ascending loop fills row 0 first.
3. Singles and pairs don't read an inside cell, so a, b, b, a and "bb" are still found: 5.
4. For "abba" (row 0, column 3) the code reads `P[1][2]`, which is still the initial False, so "abba" is missed.
5. Lesson: a wrong evaluation order often doesn't crash. It silently reads default values. Loop so that every dependency is filled first (here i descending, or by increasing length).

lessons.title: Palindromes with gaps allowed
lessons.summary: Matching ends contribute two characters around the inner answer.
lessons.body:
A palindromic subsequence may skip input characters. Keep an interval state, but compare dropping either end when they cannot both join the palindrome.

### Longest palindromic subsequence

The characters need not be next to each other, so it's a classic interval DP:

```formula essential
L[i][j] = L[i + 1][j − 1] + 2
  if i < j and s_i = s_j
L[i][j] = max(L[i + 1][j], L[i][j − 1])
  if i < j and s_i ≠ s_j
L[i][i] = 1
where
L[i][j]: the length of the longest palindromic subsequence of the characters from position i to j of s
s_i, s_j: the characters at positions i and j of s
i, j: the first and last positions of the range
max: the larger of the two values
≠: not equal to
In words: matching ends both join the palindrome (adding 2) around the best answer for the inside; otherwise drop one end and keep the better result.
```

An empty range, whose left endpoint is past its right endpoint, counts as zero. For `"bbbab"` the answer is 4 (`"bbbb"`). Its length equals the LCS length of s and its reverse; an arbitrary reconstructed LCS need not itself be palindromic. For `"acbac"` and its reverse `"cabca"`, the maximum common-subsequence length is three. Both `"aba"` and `"abc"` are longest common subsequences, but only the first is a palindrome. The equality of optimal lengths does not make every reconstructed sequence valid.

## Key takeaways
- Matching ends contribute two characters around the inner answer.
- A mismatch drops one end and keeps the better subproblem.
- Empty ranges and single positions need distinct base cases.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [Longest palindromic substring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longest_palindromic_substring)

questions.prompt: What is the length of the longest palindromic **subsequence** of `"character"`?

options.explanation: e.g. "ara" or "cac" are palindromic subsequences of length 3, but a longer one exists using both c's and both a's around the r.
4 would need an even-length palindrome such as "caac". The odd-length "carac" is longer, at 5.
Correct. "carac": c(0) a(2) r(3) a(4) c(5). The interval DP: matching ends add 2 to the inside.
"character" isn't a palindrome (it starts with c and ends with r).

questions.workedExample:
1. Indices: c0 h1 a2 r3 a4 c5 t6 e7 r8.
2. The interval rule: matching ends add 2 around the best answer for the inside; otherwise drop one end and keep the better result. A single character counts 1.

3. Look for nested matching pairs: c0…c5 encloses a2…a4, which encloses r3.
4. `L[3][3] = 1`, `L[2][4] = 1 + 2 = 3` ("ara"), `L[0][5] = L[1][4] + 2`, and `L[1][4] = 3` ("ara"), so 5.
5. Could r3…r8 do better? Between them: a4 c5 t6 e7 have no matching pairs, so that gives only 2 + 1 = 3.
6. Answer 5. The common-subsequence length with the reversed string is also five.

lessons.title: Choose non-adjacent nodes on a tree
lessons.summary: Include and exclude states separate the effect of choosing the parent.
lessons.body:
## DP on trees

Once boundary information such as the parent’s selected status is represented in the state, the relevant child subtrees can be combined independently. That makes the tree itself the DP order: compute every child before its parent (a post-order traversal).

### Maximum independent set on a tree

> Choose as many nodes as possible so that no two chosen nodes are adjacent. (Or, weighted: maximise total weight. This is "house robber on a tree".)

On general graphs this is NP-hard. On a tree with n nodes it's O(n).

**State**: two values per node v:

- `inc[v]` records best in v's subtree if v **is** chosen.
- `exc[v]` records best in v's subtree if v is **not** chosen.

**Recurrence**:

- If v is chosen, none of its children may be.
- If v isn't chosen, each child is free to be chosen or not.

```formula essential
inc[v] = w_v + Σ exc[c]   for c ∈ kids(v)
exc[v] = Σ max(inc[c], exc[c])
   for c ∈ kids(v)
answer = max(inc[r], exc[r])
where
inc[v]: the best total weight in the subtree under v when v itself is chosen
exc[v]: the best total weight in the subtree under v when v is not chosen
v: a node of the tree
w_v: the weight of node v (1 for the unweighted version)
c: a child of v
kids(v): the set of v's children
∈: "is a member of"
Σ: sum over all of v's children; 0 if v is a leaf
max: the larger of the two values
r: the root of the tree
answer: the size (or total weight) of the maximum independent set
In words: choosing v forces every child out; leaving v out lets each child independently take whichever of its two options is better.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a company party without direct bosses
> You are inviting staff to a party, and nobody enjoys a party their direct manager also attends. You want as many guests (or as much total fun) as possible. Each manager asks their team: "what's our best guest list if I go, and if I don't?"
>
> **How it maps:** the organisation chart is the tree and each person is a node. "If I go" is `inc[v]`: none of my direct reports can come, so take each report's best list without them. "If I don't" is `exc[v]`: each report independently chooses their better option. Answers flow up the chart until the top manager compares the two totals.
>
> **Where it stops:** a real organisation can have matrix management, with someone reporting to two managers. That is no longer a tree, the two sub-answers stop being independent, and the problem on a general graph is NP-hard.

```
        0
       / \
      1   2
     / \   \
    3   4   5
```

```python
def max_independent_set(adj, root=0):
    # adj: valid simple undirected tree
    if not adj:
        return 0
    if root not in range(len(adj)):
        raise ValueError("invalid root")
    def dfs(v, parent):
        inc, exc = 1, 0
        for c in adj[v]:
            # Do not walk the undirected
            # edge backwards.
            if c == parent:
                continue
            # Finish each child before its
            # parent.
            ci, ce = dfs(c, v)
            # Choosing the parent excludes
            # this child.
            inc += ce
            # An excluded parent leaves the
            # child free.
            exc += max(ci, ce)
        return inc, exc
    return max(dfs(root, -1))
```

Bottom-up on the tree above:

```
node  inc  exc
3     1    0
4     1    0
5     1    0
1     1    2      (exc: 3 and 4 free)
2     1    1
0     1+2+1=4  max(1,2)+max(1,1)=3
```

Answer 4: nodes {0, 3, 4, 5}.

For the stated valid simple undirected tree (symmetric adjacency lists, integer vertices 0..n−1), each node is visited once and each edge twice: **O(n)** work. The routine assumes this tree structure; cycles or disconnected inputs require validation or a different traversal.

> [!warning] Recursion depth on trees
> A tree can be a path of 100,000 nodes. A cold recursive Python DFS can exceed its configured call-depth limit; CPython usually starts with a limit of 1,000, but the actual threshold depends on existing call depth and implementation. For large inputs, compute an order with an explicit stack (or BFS), then process nodes in reverse order so children come before parents.

## Key takeaways
- Include and exclude states separate the effect of choosing the parent.
- Compute children before combining their answers.
- Use an explicit traversal order when recursion would be too deep.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [MIT algorithms course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/)

questions.prompt: Weighted maximum independent set on a star graph: centre node with weight 10, connected to four leaves each of weight 1. Using `inc`/`exc` tree DP, what is the answer?

options.explanation: 4 is the unweighted answer (all four leaves). With weights, the centre alone is worth more.
14 takes the centre and all leaves, but every leaf is adjacent to the centre.
11 takes the centre and one leaf, which are adjacent. If the centre is chosen, no leaf can be.
Correct. Taking the centre scores 10 and rules out every leaf; leaving it out lets all four leaves in for 4. The better is 10.

questions.workedExample:
1. Leaves: `inc = 1`, `exc = 0`.
2. Centre: choosing it scores 10 plus every leaf's `exc` (all 0), so `inc` is 10. Leaving it out lets each leaf take its better option (1), so `exc` is 4. The answer is the larger: 10.

3. Answer 10.
4. If the centre weighed 3 instead, the best value would be four, choosing the leaves rather than the weight-three centre: the DP automatically decides between "take the hub" and "take the spokes".

questions.prompt: Your recursive tree DP passes tests but crashes in production with `RecursionError` on a tree of 200,000 nodes that happens to be a long chain. What's the robust fix?

options.text: Memoise `dfs` with `@cache`
options.explanation: Each node is already visited once; caching doesn't reduce depth. The chain still needs 200,000 nested frames.

options.text: Root the tree at a leaf instead
options.explanation: For a chain, rooting at a leaf gives the deepest possible recursion. Rooting at the middle would halve it to 100,000, still far over the limit.

options.text: Switch to BFS and compute the DP in BFS order
options.explanation: BFS order visits parents *before* children, which is the wrong direction. Using its reverse is the fix; BFS order itself isn't.

options.text: Compute a traversal order with an explicit stack (or BFS), then process the nodes in reverse order so every child is finished before its parent
options.explanation: Correct. No recursion, O(n) time and memory for a tree of n nodes. Reverse BFS or reverse pre-order both guarantee children-before-parents.

questions.workedExample:
1. CPython's default limit is 1,000 frames; a chain needs one frame per node.
2. Iterative version:

This is a traversal fragment for a valid tree; replace the final ellipsis with the include/exclude updates. It produces a child-before-parent processing order, rather than computing the answer by itself.

```python
# Track parents without recursion.
order, parent = [], {root: -1}
stack = [root]
while stack:
    v = stack.pop()
    order.append(v)
    for c in adj[v]:
        if c != parent[v]:
            parent[c] = v
            stack.append(c)

# Reverse: each child comes first.
for v in reversed(order):
    ...  # children done
```

3. Every child is appended after its parent in `order`, so reversed order processes children first.
4. Raising the limit does not reduce memory or work and can be unsafe for native-recursive call paths. CPython 3.11+ avoids an extra C call for most Python-to-Python calls, but explicit traversal also removes the configured Python recursion-depth constraint.

lessons.title: Tree covers, rerooting and interval applications
lessons.summary: Excluding a vertex forces every child into a vertex cover.
lessons.body:
### Other tree DPs with the same shape

- **Tree diameter**: for each node, the two longest downward paths through different children.
- **Minimum vertex cover** (the fewest nodes such that every edge touches at least one of them): the same two states, with min instead of max. If a node is in the cover, each child takes its cheaper state; if the node is out, every child must be in, because the edge between them needs a covered end.

```formula reference
inc[v] = 1 + Σ min(inc[c], exc[c])
exc[v] = Σ inc[c]
where
inc[v]: the smallest cover of v's subtree that includes v (the 1 counts v itself)
exc[v]: the smallest cover of v's subtree that leaves v out
v: a node
c: each child of v; Σ adds over all of them (0 for a leaf)
Σ: sum over v's children
min: the smaller of the two values
In words: if a node is in the cover, every edge to its children is already covered, so each child takes its cheaper option; if the node is left out, every child must be in the cover so that the edge between them is covered.
```

- **Rerooting**: for suitable constant-sized states and O(1)-per-edge combination/exclusion (often using prefix/suffix aggregates), a second top-down pass can compute every root’s answer in O(n). More expensive transitions change the bound.

## In the real world

- **Parsing**: CYK uses an interval DP for a grammar in Chomsky normal form, in O(n³ · |G|) time for a nonempty string of n words, where |G| is the size (number of rules) of the grammar; handle an allowed empty string separately.
- **RNA secondary structure** prediction in noncrossing base-pair models (such as Nussinov and Zuker formulations) uses interval DP; unrestricted pseudoknots need other treatment.
- **Optimal binary search trees** (given access frequencies) are interval DP. Knuth (1971) observed that the best root index moves monotonically as the range of keys grows, so each range only needs to try roots between two neighbouring ranges' best roots; that cuts the work from O(n³) to O(n²) for n keys.
- **Compilers** use tree DP for instruction selection: tiling an expression tree with machine instructions at minimum cost.

## Key takeaways
- Excluding a vertex forces every child into a vertex cover.
- Rerooting is linear only with suitably cheap state combination.
- Parsing, RNA models, search trees and instruction selection use related DPs.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)
- [MIT algorithms course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/)

questions.prompt:
Minimum vertex cover on a tree (fewest nodes so that every edge touches a chosen node) uses:

```python

#   that includes v; exc[v]: one that
#   leaves v out
inc[v] = 1 + sum(min(inc[c], exc[c])
                 for c in kids[v])
exc[v] = sum(inc[c] for c in kids[v])
```

Why is `exc[v]` a sum of `inc[c]` with no `min`?

options.explanation: Not true in general: for a leaf, `exc = 0` and `inc = 1`. The reason is a constraint, not a comparison.

options.text: Because each edge (v, c) must be covered; if v is not in the cover, every child c must be
options.explanation: Correct. The edge between v and c needs at least one endpoint in the cover. With v excluded, c is forced in, so only `inc[c]` is allowed.

options.text: Because the root must always be excluded
options.explanation: The answer is `min(inc[root], exc[root])`; either choice is possible at the root.

options.text: It's a mistake; it should be `Σ min(inc[c], exc[c])`
options.explanation: That would allow both v and c to be excluded, leaving edge (v, c) uncovered.

2. v chosen: edges (v, c) are covered; each child is free → `min(inc[c], exc[c])`.
3. v not chosen: edge (v, c) must be covered by c → `inc[c]`.
4. Path 0–1–2–3–4 rooted at 0:

```
node  inc  exc
4     1    0
3     1    1
2     2    1
1     2    2
0     3    2
```

lessons.title: Represent a small set with bits
lessons.summary: Each bit records whether one item is present.
lessons.body:
Every DP so far has had states indexed by positions, lengths or weight limits. The following units cover three less obvious state spaces, then tie everything together with one idea: **a finite, acyclic DP can be evaluated over a DAG of states**. The module ends with a practical checklist for spotting DP in an interview.

## Bitmask DP

When the state needs to know **which items from a small set have been used**, encode that set as the bits of an integer (a **bitmask**): bit j is 1 if item j is in the set. Each item is either in or out, so every extra item doubles the number of possible sets: n items give 2ⁿ subsets, about a million for 20 items.

That doubling is why bitmask DP is only for small sets. Practical limits depend on how many other dimensions the state has, how many transitions each state tries, and the available memory and time. The table shows growth for a state that also records one of n endpoints with up to n transitions each (as in the travelling-salesman DP next), not a hardware guarantee.

| Items | Subsets | Endpoint slots | Work proxy |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 1,024 | ~10⁴ | ~10⁵ |
| 16 | 65,536 | ~10⁶ | ~1.7 × 10⁷ |
| 20 | ~10⁶ | ~2 × 10⁷ | ~4 × 10⁸ |
| 25 | ~3.4 × 10⁷ | ~8 × 10⁸ | ~2 × 10¹⁰ |

Each extra item multiplies the subsets by 2, and the endpoint and transition choices each add another factor of the item count, which is why the work column grows so fast.

The bit operations you need (for example, with `mask` = 11, binary `01011`, meaning items 0, 1 and 3, and `j` = 2, testing gives 0 because item 2 is absent, and adding it gives 15):

```python
mask & (1 << j)     # is j in the set?
mask | (1 << j)     # add j
mask & ~(1 << j)    # remove j
(1 << n) - 1        # the full set
bin(mask).count('1')  # set size
```

## Key takeaways
- Each bit records whether one item is present.
- The number of subsets doubles with every extra item.
- State and transition dimensions determine feasibility.

## Further reading
- [Held–Karp algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Held%E2%80%93Karp_algorithm)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

lessons.title: A visited-set state for travelling salesman
lessons.summary: Visited cities and current city determine the remaining tour choices.
lessons.body:
### Held–Karp: the travelling salesman

> Given distances between n cities, find the shortest tour that starts at city 0, visits every city exactly once, and returns.

Brute force fixes city 0 as the start and tries every order of the other n − 1 cities: (n − 1)! orders (n − 1 factorial, the product 1 × 2 × … × (n − 1)). For just 20 cities that is about 120 quadrillion tours. Hopeless.

The key observation: once you've visited a set of cities and are standing at city j, the **order** you visited them in no longer matters for the rest of the tour. Only the set and the current city do. That's the state. This DP was published independently in 1962 by Richard Bellman and by Michael Held and Richard Karp, which is why it is also called Bellman–Held–Karp.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a sales rep's ticked-off list
> A sales rep driving round a region keeps a list of towns with a tick next to each one visited. To plan the rest of the trip they need two things: which towns are ticked and where they are parked now. The order of this morning's visits is irrelevant to the cheapest way to finish.
>
> **How it maps:** the ticked list is the visited-set bitmask and the current town is j, so (ticks, current town) is the DP state. Two morning routes that end in the same town with the same ticks share one state, and only the shorter of them is worth keeping.
>
> **Where it stops:** the rep plans one trip forwards. The DP must compute an answer for every possible list of ticks and every possible current town, about n × 2ⁿ states, which is why it is only practical for roughly two dozen cities or fewer.

**State**: `dp[mask][j]` records length of the shortest path that starts at 0, visits exactly the cities in `mask`, and ends at j.

**Recurrence**: extend a path by one unvisited city k. Written "pulling" from the state before k was added:

```formula essential
dp[S ∪ {k}][k] = min(dp[S][j] + d[j][k])
   for j ∈ S, k ∉ S
dp[{0}][0] = 0
best = min(dp[F][j] + d[j][0])
   for j ≠ 0
where
dp[S][j]: the length of the shortest path that starts at city 0, visits exactly the cities in the set S, and ends at city j
S: a set of cities that includes 0 (stored as the bitmask `mask`)
S ∪ {k}: the set S with city k added (mask | 1 << k in code)
∪: union, combining two sets
{0}: the set containing only city 0 (mask 1)
j: the city where the shorter path ended, a member of S
k: the newly added city, not yet in S
∈: "is a member of"; ∉: "is not a member of"
d[j][k]: the distance from city j to city k
min: the smallest value over all the allowed choices
F: the full set of every city (the bitmask full = 2^n − 1)
n: the number of cities; the tour-closing recurrence applies for at least two cities, while zero or one city returns zero
best: the length of the shortest complete tour
≠: not equal to
In words: the cheapest way to have visited S plus k, ending at k, is the cheapest way to have visited S ending at some j, plus the hop from j to k; the tour closes with the hop back to city 0.
```

**Base**: `dp[1][0] = 0` (only city 0 visited, standing at 0). The code below "pushes" forwards instead: from each finished state it tries every unvisited k and keeps the minimum, which computes the same values.

```python
def held_karp(d):
    n = len(d)
    if any(len(row) != n for row in d):
        raise ValueError("square matrix")
    if any(type(w) is not int
           for row in d for w in row):
        raise ValueError("integer costs")
    if n <= 1:
        return 0
    INF = float('inf')
    # One set bit per city means all
    # visited.
    full = (1 << n) - 1
    dp = [[INF] * n for _ in range(1 << n)]
    # Start with only city zero visited.
    dp[1][0] = 0
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        if not mask & 1:
            continue  # tours start at 0
        for j in range(n):
            cur = dp[mask][j]
            # Skip unreachable allocated
            # table states.
            if cur == INF:
                continue
            for k in range(n):
                # A tour may not visit this
                # city again.
                if mask & (1 << k):
                    continue
                # Add one city; the numeric
                # mask increases.
                nm = mask | (1 << k)
                c = cur + d[j][k]
                # Keep the cheapest path to
                # this state.
                if c < dp[nm][k]:
                    dp[nm][k] = c
    return min(dp[full][j] + d[j][0]
               for j in range(1, n))
```

Why does increasing `mask` order work? Adding a city sets a bit, so the new mask is numerically larger. Every state is final before anything reads it.

For the four-city distance matrix

```
     0   1   2   3
0    0  10  15  20
1   10   0  35  25
2   15  35   0  30
3   20  25  30   0
```

it returns 80 (0 → 1 → 3 → 2 → 0: 10 + 25 + 30 + 15).

## Key takeaways
- Visited cities and current city determine the remaining tour choices.
- Adding a bit moves to a larger numeric mask.
- Close the full-set path by returning to city zero.

## Further reading
- [Held–Karp algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Held%E2%80%93Karp_algorithm)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

questions.prompt: Held–Karp uses the state `(set of visited cities, current city)`. Why doesn't it need to record the **order** the cities were visited in?

options.text: Because the order is recovered from the bits of the mask
options.explanation: A mask only records membership. 0 → 1 → 2 and 0 → 2 → 1 produce the same mask.

options.text: Because all orders have the same length
options.explanation: Different orders have different lengths; that's the whole problem. The DP keeps only the *shortest* one for each state.

options.text: Because the cost of finishing the tour depends only on which cities are left and where you are now, so among all paths reaching the same state only the shortest matters
options.explanation: Correct. That's optimal substructure. Replacing a path with a shorter one to the same state can only improve the final tour.

options.text: Because TSP distances are symmetric
options.explanation: Held–Karp works on asymmetric distances too. Symmetry isn't what makes order irrelevant.

questions.workedExample:
1. Two partial tours: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 (length 40) and 0 → 2 → 1 → 3 (length 55).
2. Both have visited {0, 1, 2, 3} and stand at 3.
3. Every way to finish from here is available to both, at the same cost.
4. So the 55 path can never be part of an optimal tour that the 40 path couldn't beat. Discard it.
5. That collapses every ordering into one state per (visited set, current city) pair: about n × 2ⁿ states for n cities, instead of (n − 1)! orders. For sixteen cities, that is about one million allocated states against about 1.3 trillion fixed-start orders.

lessons.title: Count Held–Karp work and storage
lessons.summary: Held–Karp reduces factorial enumeration to exponential DP.
lessons.body:
The visited-set recurrence is exact for the stated cost matrix. Its resource requirements depend on the table representation and on which states are reachable.

Let n be the number of cities. The allocated table has one slot per subset of cities and possible end city: n × 2ⁿ slots. Each reachable state tries up to n next cities, so the work is at most about n² × 2ⁿ steps. So **O(n² · 2ⁿ) time, O(n · 2ⁿ) space**.

For 20 cities that is about 420 million steps, against about 1.2 × 10¹⁷ brute-force tours: roughly 300 million times fewer. It is a work bound, not this implementation's exact transition count, because many allocated states are never reached.

The two growth rates also respond differently to one more city. Adding a city a little more than doubles the Held–Karp work (twice as many subsets, slightly more cities per state), but multiplies the brute-force tour count by the number of cities. Memory grows as fast as the table, which is often the first limit you hit.

Held–Karp remains exponential, but its bound is much smaller than factorial enumeration. NP-hardness does not prove that every exact TSP algorithm must take exponential time; even a proof that polynomial-time solving differs from polynomial-time verification would rule out polynomial time, not every subexponential possibility. Concorde uses branch-and-cut techniques and has solved particular large benchmark instances, which is not a worst-case guarantee.

## Key takeaways
- Held–Karp reduces factorial enumeration to exponential DP.
- Allocated table states and executed transitions are different counts.
- Memory layout and available resources matter as much as the growth bound.

## Further reading
- [Held–Karp algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Held%E2%80%93Karp_algorithm)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

options.text: Both roughly double, because one city is added
options.explanation: Brute force doesn't double: every existing tour order can now have the new city inserted in many places. Its count multiplies by 16.

options.text: Held–Karp a little more than doubles (about 2.3×); brute force multiplies by 16
options.explanation: Correct. Held–Karp gains a factor of 2 from the subsets and a little from the extra city per state. Brute force's (n − 1)! grows by the factor n − 1 = 16.

options.text: Held–Karp multiplies by 17; brute force doubles
options.explanation: That reverses the two behaviours. Factorial growth is the one that multiplies by the number of cities.

options.text: Neither changes much, because one city is a small change
options.explanation: Both are exponential or worse in n, so one more city always matters. The question is by how much.

4. Held–Karp is still exponential: each extra city roughly doubles the work and the memory, which is what eventually limits it.

lessons.title: Assignments, submasks and profiles
lessons.summary: A job mask can describe which assignments remain.
lessons.body:
Bitmasks also represent assigned jobs or the occupied boundary of a grid. The mask must retain every fact needed by later choices, not merely count how much work is done.

### Other bitmask DPs

- **Assignment problem**: n workers, n jobs, cost matrix. `dp[mask]` records minimum cost to assign the first `popcount(mask)` workers (popcount is the number of 1 bits in the mask) to the jobs in `mask`. O(n · 2ⁿ). (The Hungarian algorithm does it in O(n³), but the bitmask DP generalises to constraints Hungarian can't handle.)
- **Set cover / partition into groups**: iterate submasks with `sub = (sub - 1) & mask`, stopping explicitly after zero (otherwise it wraps back to mask). Looping over every mask and all its submasks visits 3ⁿ pairs for n items, because each item independently plays one of three roles: outside the mask, in the mask but not the submask, or in both. That is about 14 million pairs for 15 items, far fewer than the 4ⁿ pairs of two unrelated masks. Each extra item multiplies the work by 3. Transitions may still add work per pair.
- **Profile DP** (broken-profile, e.g. tiling a grid with dominoes): the mask records which cells of the current column boundary are already filled.

## When assignments interact

The plain job mask is sufficient only when assignment costs depend on the current engineer and chosen project. If adjacent engineers’ project choices interact, also retain the previous engineer’s project. The engineer index is the mask’s set-bit count; the last-project flag supplies the missing boundary information. With n projects this gives O(n × 2ⁿ) allocated states and up to n next choices each, hence O(n² × 2ⁿ) transition work. A mask alone would incorrectly merge histories with different neighbouring costs.

## Key takeaways
- A job mask can describe which assignments remain.
- Extra interaction constraints may require additional boundary state.
- Stop a submask loop after zero to avoid wrapping around.

## Further reading
- [Held–Karp algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Held%E2%80%93Karp_algorithm)
- [Erickson: dynamic programming](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/03-dynprog.pdf)

options.text: 4, because there are 2ⁿ masks and up to 2ⁿ submasks each

options.text: 16, because the work grows with the number of items

options.explanation: Correct. An item is outside the mask, in the mask but not the submask, or in both. Adding an item multiplies the number of pairs by 3: about 14 million pairs for 15 items, about 43 million for 16.

1. A pair (mask, sub) with sub inside mask gives each item one of three roles: not in the mask; in the mask but not in sub; or in sub (and so in the mask).
2. The roles are chosen independently, so the number of pairs is 3 multiplied by itself once per item: 3ⁿ.
3. One more item therefore multiplies the count by 3. For 15 items that is about 14 million pairs; for 16 about 43 million; for 20 about 3.5 billion.
